ChapterOne
The State, Conflict Resolution, and Development in Africa
K. O. Ilol F N. Onahl N. E Agujiobil O.P Uba-Uzoagwua] J. Ohabuenyil C. O. Ugwu
Introduction
The relationship between peace, conflict, and development has become a central
concern in contemporarydevelopmentdiscourse.Peaceis widely acknowledged asa
prerequisite for sustainable development, as it creates an enabling environment for
economic productivity, social cohesion, and political stability. Conversely, violent
conflict undermines state capacity,erodes public trust in institutions,and diverts scarce
resources from development priorities toward security expenditure and humanitarian
relief(UNDP,2023).Inrecognitionofthisrelationship,theUnitedNations Sustainable
Development Goal (SDG) 16 emphasizes the promotion of peaceful and inclusive
societies, access to justice, and the strengthening of institutions as foundations for
sustainable development.
Given its position as the preeminent political organization in the society, the
responsibility mediating and resolving societal conflicts to allow for the pursuit of
development rests squarely with the state.FromAristotle's conception of the state as
thehighestform of human association to contemporaryAfricandebates on security and
legitimacy, the state remains central to conflict resolution and development.
Significantly, African states face persistent challenges in resolving conflicts within
their borders as a result of which the development enterprise has been imperiled in
much of the continent. In this chapter, we explore in detail the nexus between the state,
conflict resolution and development in Africa with a view to highlighting those
challenges andprescribing solutions for overcoming them.For clarity,the chapter is
presented as follows: first is the conceptualization of the state; second, we highlight the
peculiarities of the state in Africa; third we explore the interface between conflict and
the challenges of development in Africa,then we examine the state and conflict
resolution in Africa citing some case studies; and finally, is the conclusion.
Understanding the State
In spite of its centrality, the state has often been considered as a very slippery or
confusing concept. This is partly due to the synonymous use of the state with other
concepts such as government, nation-state or country. In some cases, state is compared
with political regime or economic system.Moreover, over the years, the concept, nature
and functions of state have undergone considerable changes due to numerous politico-
historical developments (Roy, 2025).
From antiquity,philosophershave sought todefine whatdistinguishes the statefrom
otherformsofsocial life.ThefoundingFatherofPolitical Science,Aristotle(384-322
BC).defined the state as a union of families and villages having for its end perfect and
self-sufficient life. In his book, Politics [Book I], Aristotle stated that:

This observation underscores the unique role of the state as the highest form of human
association, tasked with pursuing the collective good.
His definition of state mirrors idea and functioning of the Greek city-states which were
small in size. The English political theorist and economist, Harold J. Laski (1893-1950)
in his book, An Introduction to Politics, defined the state as a “territorial society divided

(1926), sought to distinguish the state from other kinds of associations. He stated that
the state embraces the whole of people in a specific territory and it has the special
function of maintaining social order.According to him, the state performs this function
through its agent, the government "which speaks with the voice of law". Similarly,
R.M. Maclver and C.H. Page in their book, Society: An Introductory Analysis (1950,
exclusive investment with the final power of coercion".
Max Weber (1864-1920), a famous German sociologist, sought to evolve a
'sociological' definition of the state. From a sociological perspective, he defined the
state as a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate
use of physical force within a given territory'.
Asused in political science,the word state meansa community or society politically
organized under one independent government within a definite territory and subject to
no outside control. There can be no community without the people to form one, and no
common life without some definite piece of territory to live in.When people livea
collective life, they fulfil the meaning of Aristotle's famous phrase, "Man is a social
animal" and when they live a settled life on a definite territory to realize the purpose of
collective living,they fulfil the meaning of Aristotle's second famous phrase,"Man is
a political animal".The people are bound by rules of common behaviour and their
violation is accompanied by punishment. That is the state. Society meets man's
companionship; the state solves the problem created by such companionship.
particularlythat ofitsterritorial connection and of its useoffered.It is charged withthe
duty tomaintain those conditions of lifefor whichthe state came into existenceandfor
which it continues to exist.
Therefore, the state is a natural, a necessary, and a universal institution. It is natural
because it is rooted in the reality of human nature. It is necessary because, according to

Aristotle, "The state comes into existence originating in the bare needs of life and
continuing in existence for the sake of good life". Man needs the state to satisfy his
diverse needs and to be what he desires to be. Without the state he cannot rise to the
full stature ofhis personality.In fact,in the absence ofsuch a controlling and regulating
authority, society cannot be held together and there will be disorder and anarchy. What
food means to the human body the state means to man. Both areindispensable for his
existence and developmient. The state exists whenever and wherever man has lived in
and organized society.
It is significant that though some sort of political Organisation has existed since ancient
times, such as Greek city-states and the Roman empire, the contemporary concept of
the state owes its origin to Nicollo Machiavelli (1469-1527) who in his book, The
Prince (1513) expressed the idea of the state as 'the power which has authority over
men' (Machiavelli, 2003. He viewed the state as the supreme human association,
focusing on power, stability, and survival, often disregarding traditional morality to
prevent political decay.
Perspectives on the State
In modern political'theory, the significance of the concept of the state has been
fluctuating. Some exponents of the behavioural approach in political science even
suggested abandoning the concept of the state altogether. Their main objectlon is that
this concept does not help in understanding political reality or the political process,
because the term 'state' refers to a formal concept while real politics transcends the
formal organizationofthestate.
: The emergence of the liberalism and the Marxian political philosophy was marked by
renewed interests in the study ofstate.In essence,twobroadperspectiveshaveemerged
for the explanation of the state namely: Liberalism and Marxism. The idea of liberalism
was advocated by John Locke, the 17th century English political philosopher. Locke
put forwarded three principles of liberalism - right to life, liberty and private property
which were considered as natural rights. The liberal philosophy is based on the
principles of individual freedom, freedom of choice, non-interference and limited
power of the state. According to the liberal perspective, consent should be the basis of
state not force.
At the core of Liberalism is the belief in a harmonious society where individuals can
pursue their interests freely. The state, from a liberal perspective, acts as a neutral
arbiter that ensures the smooth functioning of society. It provides the framework within
which individuals can coexist peacefully, resolving conflicts through laws and
regulationsratherthanforce.
Liberals place a strong emphasis on constitutional mechanisms to control state power.
They argue that a well-designed constitution can prevent the abuse of power by
dividing it among various branches of government, such as the executive, legislative,
Scanned with

[Page 4]
and judiciary. This systeim of checks and balances ensures that no single entity can
dominate the state,protecting individual freedoms andrights.
Anotherkey aspect of the Liberal perspective is the role of civil society.Civil society
comprises variousiorganizations,institutions,andmovementsthatoperate
independentlyofthestate.Theseentitiesprovideaplatformforindividualstoexpress
their interests, engage in collective action, and hold the state accountable. In this view,
a vibrant civil society is essential for maintaining a healthy democracy and preventing
theconcentration ofpowerinthehands ofthestate(PolSci Institute,2025).
Basedonthese,Lockeadvocatedthe social contracttheoryofthestate,whichseesthe
state as a social contract between the citizens and the leaders.As it relates to societal
conflict, the liberal perspective views the state as a neutral arbiter, protecting individual
rights and ensuring social harmony, often operating as a "common good" institution.
Marxism is a set of political and economic principles based on the philosophy of Karl
Marx(1818-1884),theGerman born political philosopher and his friend Friedrich
Engels (1820-1895). It emerged as a response to the classical liberal ideas or doctrine
of laissez-faire and free market economy that created a tiny section of privileged class
at the expense of huge number of working-class resulting inequality and injustice.
ContrarytotheLiberal perspective,Marxisttheorists view thestateas an instrument of
class domination. According to Marxism, the state serves the interests of the ruling
classes, whether they are feudal lords or capitalists.It functions to maintain the existing
class structure and perpetuatetheexploitation ofthe working class
Central to Marxist theory is theconcept of class struggle.Marxists argue that history is
drivenbythe conflictbetween different social classes.Thestate,in this context,is seen
as a tool used by the ruling class to suppress the working class and prevent them from
achieving class consciousness.Class consciousness refers to the awareness of one's
social and economic position and the recognition of the need for collective action to
challengetheexisting power structure.
Marxists also highlight the repressive nature ofthe state in.maintaining class hegemony.
The state employs various means, such as the police, military, and legal system, to
working class from challenging the existing order and to ensure the continued
dominance of the ruling class.In his book The German Ideology (1846), Marx
perceived the modern state as a product serving the interests of the bourgeoise.
Similarly, in The Communist Manifesto (1848) which was published two years later,
Marx and Engels observed that'modern state's executive functions as a committee to
oversee the collective interests of the bourgeoisie, representing the ruling capitalist
class,

The primarydifference betwcen the Liberal and Marxistperspectives lies in their views
on the role of the state. While Liberals see the state as a neutral arbiter that promotes
harmony and protects individual freedoms, Marxists view it as a tool of class
domination that perpetuates exploitation and suppresses dissent:Also, both
perspectives emphasize the importance of controlling state power, but they advocate
different mechanisms for achieving this goal. Liberals focus on constitutional
mechanisms and the role of civil society, while Marxists emphasize the inevitability of
class struggle and the eventual overthrow of the ruling class by the exploited class to
achieve a more just and equitable society (PolSci Institute, 2025).
TheStateinAfrica
Historically, what we know as the modern African States were created by European
colonial powers most especially, Britain, France, Spain, Portugal, German and Italy.
Although, the enduring colonial powers with large colonies were Britain and France.
Africa as a continent was partitioned by Colonial powers in Berlin during what is
regarded as the Berlin Conference of 1884/5. It was in this conference that Africa was
wholesomely shared among colonial masters, without taking in considerations local
conditions and internal political dynamics. The consequence of this singular action by
European powers redirected the destiny of the African people. Sworn enemies were
grouped together in a single colony, an ethnic group were divided along different
colonies and ,owned" by different masters (Harris, 1987, p. 166-167). What is more,
after independence African nationalists retained this structure and its underlining
territories by their erstwhile colonial masters in what is referred as neocolonialism.
Fromtheabove,it isveryclear that theAfricanStatesdid notorganicallyemergefrom
African society unlike is the case with the history of other States in the international
system. Also, African States were not created to advance the course of Africans but to
perpetuate the interest of European Powers. In order words, due to the peculiar
circumstances of their creation,African States were not set up in the firstplace,for
African development. Rather, it was an arena for exploitation for the purpose of
developing the European Metropoles. This situation has been described as the African
tragedy as it has continued to fan toxic politics in the African States which is
underminingtheirdevelopmentandauthenticprogress.
And as stated in theprevious section,theuniversalcharacteristicsofmodern States are:
Sovereignty, population, government, and territory. If we use the attribute of
sovereignty,for instance, to interrogate the nature ofthe African states, we are likely to
find them wanting. As an attribute of the state, sovereignty refers to non-intervention
'intheaffairs of thestateby external powers.Statesovereignty is a central concept in
international law,which refers tothe exclusive authority and autonomy ofa state to
govern itself without external interference.Established in international law throughthe
1648 Peace of Westphalia, sovereignty represents the idea of supreme, independent

authority within a defined territory. It is the right of sovercign states to be recognized
by other States and gives a State the right to relate with other countries on an cqual
footing irrespective of size. This right further confers on a State the right to freely enter.
into diplomatic and trade relations with other States. This is always cvidenced in the
conduct of each sovereign state viewed from the perspective of economics, politics,
culture, religion, etc (Amaefule, 2024).
Sovereignty has both internal and external dimensions. Internal sovereignty refers to
supreme authority over citizens and territory, while external sovereignty involves
independence from foreign control. Even though sovereignty is not absolute, in the
specific case of African states, their sovereignty has been constrained by a number of.
factors, including ethnic diversity, external interference by former colonial masters
(Loshkariov, 2024), and the erosion of state borders by forces of globalization, which
have made it quite difficult for national governments to exercise full control over their
domestic economies and political processes (Mbaku, 2018).
Another recent development which has tended to erode the sovereignty of African
states is the doctrine of the Responsibility to Protect (R2P). The new doctrine was
introduced to prevent and stop mass atrocity crimes such as genocide, war crimes,
ethnic cleansing, and crimes against humanity as occurred in Rwanda and Bosnia in
the 1990s.
Conflict and the Challenges of Development in Africa
Conflict and development are deeply intertwined, with the state at the center of both
processes. Security is a prerequisite for development, as instability undermines
infrastructure, displaces populations, and erodes trust in institutions (Collier, 2007).
Conversely, development initiatives can generate conflict when they marginalize
communities, particularly in resource extraction projects (Mkandawire, 2001). The
state's role is to balance these linkages by promoting inclusive growth and equitable
resource distribution (Francis, 2006).
Conflicts in Africa are diverse and interconnected, The dynamics of African conflicts
are best understood when viewed against the backdrop of the historical, political and
international contexts within which they occur (Eferebo, 2023). First, the perennial
conflicts plaguing many ofAfrican countries have rightly been attributed to the corrupt
leadership, poverty, unemployment, frustration and alienation of the vibrant youths in
many states of Africa, It has further been argued that most countries of the Africa are
plural societies in the grip of strong centrifugal forces. They are divided along religious
and ethnic fault lines and so are often polarized. As a result, they are prone to violence,
exhibit atavistic nationalism, engage in territorial disputes and struggle over natural
resources. Ake (1992, p.15) argued that the satellization of the South by the wealthier
nations of the North is another source of division and conflict in the South, now and
then it leads to proxy wars".

During colonial subjugation, previously independent and diverse ethnic nationalities

to remain in power, resorted to ethnicity, and its twin vice, corruption,
Citing the example of Nigeria, Eze et al. (2024) observed that Nigeria, which is by far
Africa's most populous country is also endowed with enormous natural resource
deposits, including oil and gas as well as several tonnes of solid mineral deposits that
regional and continental player and putatively an important player on the global scene.
The, however, informed that the country's potentials have been greatly circumscribed
by its mosaic of ethnic and religious configurations. The country is made up of over
two hundred and fifty ethnic groups and is delicately balanced on a twin religious and

Eze el al noted that currently, the two most serious sources of rupture in the country

insurgents who have been ravaging the Northeast and other parts of Northern Nigeria
since2009;and second,is the deadly nomadic Fulani herdsmenwhohave been

They noted that even though the herders had clashed with crop farmers even in Muslim-
dominated areas like the North West of Nigeria, in recent years their attacks have been
concentrated on farming communities in the North Central and Southern parts of the
country both of which have predominantly Christian populations and a sizable
population of traditionalists. Both the Christians and the traditionalists are, therefore,
thought to be the targets of a wider Islamization agenda being systematically executed
through the herders (Eze et al, 2024).
Another point of emphasis is the phenomenon of “failed states" syndrome. The
existence of the state is a function of the social control it can exercise over its territory.
This is in the sense that the more social control a state is able to exercise, the more it
can mobilize all of its citizenry to promote overall development and gain tremendous
capacity in engaging external forces, (Mabogunje, 1996). The structural weakness
prevalent in many African states is reflective of the failure of the leadership to exercise
control due to its illegitimate basis of authority. And the inability of the state to enforce
compliance to its laws and the failure to mobilize the human and material resources for
economic development provides the incendiary for conflicts to strive (Eferebo, 2023).
Of significant concern is the internationalization of African conflicts as the world is
driven by forces of globalization.Among other things, economic interests and struggle
for resources African conflicts are exploited by the big powers for their own selfish
interests. A typical example is the Mano River region (Liberia and Sierra Leone) where
civil wars raged for many years fueled by the quest for exploitation of their resources
by external powers.The involvement of foreign interests in the conflicts has led to the
supply and proliferation of Small Arms and Light Weapons (SALWs) in the area in
exchange for money from the sale ofprecious minerals like diamonds, gold, rubber and
timber (Twaddle, 1996:10).
Similarly, the current spate of banditry and terrorism ravaging Nigeria's northern region
cannot be completely divorced from the role offoreign interests over the exploitation
of numerous precious mineral deposits within the region.Also, the involvement of
external combatants in the insurgency in Nigeria's North East has also been widely

Arguably, social conflicts create four undesirable dimensions the have serious
repercussion for development namely: the nonproductive consumption of resources;
disintegration of social systems; production and maintenance of dissociative
sentiments; and the development of social and individual problems (Himes, 1980).
Each of these dimensions neither promotes political stability nor socioeconomic
development. For instance, the non-productive consumption of resources results in
wastages. Also, funds that could have been used for the provision of infrastructures
would be channeled for the acquisition of armaments, and destruction of lives and
property in conflicts are wasteful efforts. Thus, functioning of the social system in a
conflict situation, 'cannot be positive because families are broken down while
productive activities cannot be undertaken and eventually social community could
disintegrate as evidenced by the collapseofthestate in some conflict situation inAfrica
(Mohammed, 1997:128).
Significantly, sustained conflict as experienced in much of Africa wreaks havoc on the
properties, but it ultimately necessitates the reallocation of resources from
infrastructural development towards replacement,rehabilitation or reconstruction of
damaged social amenities after the conflict. Violent conflicts disrupt the process of
production, create conditions for pillage of the countries' resources and divert their
application from development purposes to servicing war. Violent conflict is thus
responsible for perpetuating misery and underdevelopment in the continent, The point
of emphasis is that the conflict destabilizes peaceful and harmonious relationships
between conflicting parties and undermines development by creating objective
conditions that leads as well as enhance poverty, unemployment and inequality in the
African continent. Also, conflicts lead to spike in social problems such as crimes, drug
addition, prostitution, rape,divorce and starvation,which in turn ignite more conflicts
that hampers peace and development in any nation (Eferebo, 2023).
Nextier SPD (2020) observed that development is uniquely knotted to violent
extremism.When development is in deficit, it stokes embers of violence as
economically deprived groups seek measures, often violent, to salvage their
vulnerabilitie's. On the other hand, development programmes are valuable in preventing
extremism. In the words of United Nations Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres, the
creation of open, equitable, inclusive, and pluralist societies, based on the full respect
andmeaningful alternative to violent extremism.
Underdevelopment remains at the core of violent extremism that leads to conflict in
most developing countries. Ranging from some factors, the inability of developing
nations to navigate their resources towards growth, protection, and meeting of other

As noted above, Nigeria has had an unfair share of violent conflict with the Boko
Haram insurgency, the menace of armed banditry, farmers-herders conflict, inter-
communal and inter-religious wars, land wars, gang wars, and kidnapping activities.
This is in addition to its poverty situation and growing population. These issues have
expanded developmental probleims in the country and weakened the state's capacity to
engender a good living standard for the citizens. The situation of underdevelopment
and extreme poverty fuels group struggle over resources. Factors such as corruption,
exclusion, patrimonialism, and other governance failures are the root causes of
underdevelopment, and therefore trigger violent conflicts. Tlhus, the state becomes
incapable of addressing both the development issues and the resultant conflicts (Nextier
SPD, 2020).

The State and Conflict Resolution inAfrica
Recalling our earlier conceptualizations of the state,the most commonly used
definition is that by Max Weber who describes "the state as a compulsory political
organization with a centralized government that maintains a monopoly of the legitimate
use of force within a certain territory(cited in Cudworth et al., 2007,p.95).Weber
buttresses that the state"is a human community that (successfully)claims the monopoly
of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory" (Weber, 1991, p.78).
Related to this is that the state is a public force, which emerged from the society and is
standing above the society,to mediate the conflicts within the society and keep it within
the bounds oforder (Engels, 1909).The state, therefore, acts as a primary mediator and
arbiter in conflict resolution, using mechanisms like formal courts, security agencies,
and policy dialogue to manage violence and promote stability. These mechanisms
provide structured avenues for conflict management, ranging from binding legal
judgments to collaborative peacebuilding initiatives (Patten, 2023),
 Building on this philosophical foundation, contemporary African scholars have
expandedthe discoursebylinking the state to the concept of security.According to one
of those scholars, security has become a big issue in Africa today because of the various
forns of carnage, brutality, pogroms, and even genocide associated with incessant civil
wars and other forms of violent conflicts on the continent (Nnoli 2006). Nnoli noted that
the collapse or near collapse of states has made physical safety the preeminent concerm of
most Africans. The state is no longer able to generate the fundamental conditions for the
protection of life. This disintegration of the security arrangement of African states has
produced serious discussions about the concept of national security andits underlying
relations of power. It has demonstrated the failure of the African states to link the security
of theirregimes to the physical security of their citizens,as well as the failureto guarantee
the security ofeven their regimes.In other words, it would seemthat African states are yet
to realize that the best guarantee of state security is the security of their citizens, and the
willing acceptance by the latter of the political rules of the game on which the legitimacy
ofthe state rests. In line with this new thinking, the relevant questions currently being asked
in security circles include: Who are the protectors? What is being protected? From whom
is the protection? Who decides when national security has been achieved7 (Nnoli 2006,
p.7),

In the light of the above, Nnoli (2006) observed, “as a concept, national security
(security in short) seems to have acquired a mystique. In the minds of most people, it
has become mystical, mythical, even mysterious..." (p. 1). He further argued that this
mystification of national security has given rise to “"intellectual uncertainty, analytical
confusion, paradigmatic disorder, and theoretical impotence" (Nnoli, 2006, p. 5). Thus,
whileAristotle emphasizes the state's pursuit ofthe highest good, Nnoli draws attention
to the complexities and ambiguities surrounding the state's responsibility for security
in modern Africa. Together, these insights frame the state as both a philosophical ideal
and a practical institution whose effectiveness in conflict resolution and development
depends on its ability to provide clarity, legitimacy and protection of its citizens for
sustainable development (Ake, 1996). However, in Africa, the state's capacity to
perform these functions is often limited, leading to persistent conflict and
underdevelopment (Herbst,2000).
Partof the problem with security in Africa is that, as captured bytheUnited Nations
Development Program's Human Development Report 1994:
The concept of security has for too long been interpreted narrowly as
security of territory from external aggression, or as protection of
national interests inforeignpolicy oras global security from the threat
of nuclear holocaust. It has been related to nation states more than
people...(UNDP 1994, p.22).
This observation gave rise to the concept of human security in place of nation security.
As enunciated in the 1994 UNDP landmark report, unlike national security, human
security is a people-centered approachthat shifts thefocus from protectingthestate's
borders to protecting individuals.It isfundamentallydefined as"freedomfromfearand
freedom from want," aiming to safeguard human dignity and well-being from a wide
array of threats (UNDP, 1994). The then UN Secretary-General, Kofi Annan, reckoned
that freedom from want, freedom from fear, and the freedom of future generations to
inherit a healthy natural environment together constitute the interrelated building
blocks of human-and therefore national- security (Musah 2009).
The report highlighted four characteristics of human security namely: universal;
people-centred; interdependent; and early prevention. It further outlined seven
interconnected elements of security: economic, food, health, environmental, personal,
community and political.
Economic Security: Protection from unemployment, income inequality, and
sudden poverty.
Food Security: Assured physical and economic access to basic food.
Health Security: Protection against diseases and unsafe environments.
Environmental Security: Protection from environmental degradation, resource
depletion,and natural disasters.
Personal Security: Protection from physical violence, crime, and domestic
abuse.
12
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 13]
Community Security:Survival of traditional relationships and values, and
protection from cthnic discrimination.
Political Security: Protection of basic human rights and freedoms from state
repression (UNDP, 1994).
In what he described as security hazard in African countries, Hutchful (1998) considered
the use of govermance,economic development and legitimate force to subjugate fellow
citizens as the common factor of insecurity in Africa. According to him, there is sufficient
evidence to demonstrate that governance is monopolized by ethnic or ideological
oligarchies at the expense of the majority. of ordinary citizens who are frequently
victimized. According to this position, political exclusion, economic marginalization, and
social discrimination threaten the security of citizens to such an extent that they regard the
stateas the primary threatto their survival.In desperation, the citizens take the laws into
their own hands as a means of safeguarding their fundamental values from the threat of
unacceptable govermment policies. People who believe that the government ino longer
represents their best interests seek, by all means to overthrow it or otherwise establish an
alternative state. Hutchful further argued that though the decline of the state as the
guarantor of protection and human.security is serious, its role as the creator of insecurity
is even more serious.
In additionto theabove,Africanstatesfacemultiple challenges in fulfillingtheirroles
in conflict resolution and development. Weak institutions, leadership deficits, and
while global powers and multinational corporations complicate conflict resolution
(Zartman, 1995). Herbst (2000) argues that many African states lack the infrastructural
power to project authority across their territories, leading to persistent instability.
Bayart (2009) highlights the politics of patronage, where leaders prioritize personal
networks over collective welfare,undermining the Aristotelian vision of the state as a
pursuit of the highest good. Englebert (2000) emphasizes that legitimacy is not merely
about recognition byother states but also about the ability of governments to command
loyalty from their citizens. Without legitimacy, the state cannot effectively mediate
conflictorfosterdevelopment.
Ioryue (2025) argues that leadership'strategies are critical for peacebuilding, as
effective leaders can mobilize resources, foster dialogue, and build trust among
conflicting parties. The lack of visionary leadership has often left African states
vulnerable to crises.Moreover,external interference byglobal powersand
multinational corporations complicates conflict resolution, as foreign interests often
prioritize resourceextraction over stability.
Meanwhile, the point needs to be made that the challenges confronting African states
are not insurmountable. Rather, prospects for improvement lie in strong leadership,
institutional reforms, and regional cooperation. Effective leaders can mobilize
13
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 14]
resources, foster dialogue, and build trust among conflicting partics, iaying the
foundation for sustainable peace. Institutional reforins can strengthen governance,
while regional cooperation can enhance collective security.
Case Studies:Rwanda,Nigcria,and South Africa
The experiences of Rwanda, Nigeria, and South Africa illustrate both the potential and
limitations of state-led conflict resolution and development. Rwanda demonstrates how
strong state-led reconciliation mechanisms can foster stability. Following the 1994
genocide, the government established Gacaca courts to promote justice and
reconciliation. Clark (2010) argues that these courts, despite limitations, contributed to
rebuilding trust and fostering development.Rwanda's experience shows that inclusive
state mechanisms can transform conflict into opportunities for national healing.
South Africa offers a different model through its Truth and Reconciliation Commission
(TRC). Hayner (2002) argues that the TRC promoted healing by addressing identity-
based conflicts rooted in apartheid.While not without criticism,theTRC demonstrated
how inclusive state mechanisms can foster national unity and deyelopment. South
Africa's experience underscores the importance oflegitimacy and inclusivity in conflict
resolution.
Nigeria, on its part, illustrates the challenges of weak state capacity. Nigeria presents a
compelling illustration of the peace-development nexus, Since attaining independence
in 1960, the country's development trajectory has been repeatedly disrupted by violent
conflicts. The Nigerian civil war (1967-1970) marked a defining moment in the
nation's history, leaving profound political, cconomic, and social scars, Although the
war formally ended with the declaration of"No Victor, No Vanquished," the absence
of a comprehensive reconciliation process meant that many grievances remained
unresolved. These unresolved tensions have continued to manifest in various forms of
conflict across the country (Akoji, Gabriel, Kosok, & Oduntan, 2026).
Similarly, in contemporary Nigeria, insecurity remains pervasive and multifaceted. The
Boko Haram insurgency in the northeast has resulted in tens of thousands of deaths, the
displacement of millions, and the destruction of schools, hospitals, and livelihoods. In
the Niger Delta, militancy driven by gricvances over resource control, environmental
degradation, and perceived marginalization has disrupted oil production and
undermined national revenue. In the Middle Belt, farmer-herder clashes--cxacerbated
by climate change, desertification, and population pressure have claimed numerous
lives and destroyed rural economies, Electoral violence, particularly during highly
competitive elections, further undermines democratic consolidation and public
confidence in governance (Akinwale, 2010; Okoli & Atelhe, 2014).
The Global Peace Index consistently ranks Nigeria among the least peaceful countries
globally, reflecting the scale and persistence of insecurity and governance challenges
(Institute for Economics & Peace, 2022). This persistent instability highlights the
14
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 15]
urgent nced for effective conflict management mechanisms and long-term peace
building strategies (Akoji, Gabricel, Kosok, & Oduntan, 2026),
The Boko Haram insurgency has exposcd the inability of the Nigerian state to provide
sccurity and development in its norhern regions.Agbiboa (2015)notes that corruption,
poor governance, and lack of regional cooperation have hindered efforts to address
terrorism.Nigeria's case highlights the importance ofinstitutional reforms and regional
collaboration in addressing complex conflicts.
Together, these cases reveal that state-led initiatives can succeed when grounded in
legitimacy,inclusivity,and institutional capacity.They also show that failures often
stem from weak institutions, corruption, and lack of cooperationgri2ildlu
Summary and Concluslon
From the foregoing presentation, it could be scen that the state in Africa is both a
philosophical ideal and a practical institution.Its effectiveness in conflict resolution
and development depends on legitimacy, institutional strength, and inclusive
governance. Casc studies show both successes, such as Rwanda and South Africa, and
failures, such as Nigeria, underscoring the importance of leadership and cooperation.
The state remains pivotal in shaping Africa's future. Philosophically, it embodies the
pursuit ofthe highest good.Practically,it is the primary actor in conflict resolution and
development. But currently, the state has failed to live up to these twin responsibilities
in much of the continent. The importance of lcadership, institutional reforms, and
regional cooperation for addressing these challenges have been amply highlighted in
literature, However, we wish to add, following Ngwu, Nwosumba and Onah (2024)
that overcoming the leadership challenge requires the deliberate self-rcawakening of
African intellectuals to assume their historic role of awakening their various societies.
This is because, it is only through such self and other awakening that African societies
can muster the necessaryforce that will compel behavioral change among the current
generation of decadent leaders that have beggared their people since independence, It
is only with the emergence of good leadership that far-reaching institutional reforms
can be pursued and meaningful regional cooperation achieved.

strategies in Nigeria. African Journal on Conflict Resolution, 10(3), 123-140

chapters.content:
[Page 16]
Chapter Two
EthnicandCommunal ConflictsinAfrica
J. E. Nvofial B. O. Ugvul K. T. Ezeugwiul P. E. Ezemel O. Amyoko-Shaba
Introduction
All African countries as they exist today were created by the European colonial powers
that arbitrarily brought together disparate ethnic nationalities into distinct political
entities. The colonial governments did little to integrate the diverse groups so as to
overcome their primordial differences.The cleavages crystallized into relationships of
attrition, which came to the fore when the African States gained independence.
After decades of self-rule, Africa remains a hotbed of conflicts with ethnicity at the
root. This is primarily because individual group members built their identities around
their cthnic groups rather than the state. The obvious implication is that the members'
loyalty is primarily to their ethnic group, while the nation comes second. The individual
identitiesfurthercoalesceintoacommon ethnicidentitythatprovidestheplatformfor
solidarity and mobilization for ethnic group resources. The resources, in this context,
refer to the use of a people's collective identity to successfully get more than their fair
share of the social pie or benefits. This situation led Hoffiman and Patel (2017, p. vi)
local and not nationalThey further explained that"there is a deep-seated lack of
confidence in oficial institutions, or in the universal application of a fair and neutral
rule of law". This severely weakens the consolidation of a Nigerian national identity
based on common and equal citizenship and instead, less effective social contracts are
forged particularly around ethnic or religious identities - an arrangement that fuels
intercommunaldistrust.
This chapter examines the phenomenon of ethnicity, the underlying theories of
ethnicity,andhowethnicity helps in constructing ethnic identitythatdrives conflicts in
Africa. The second section showcases some specific case studies of communal conflicts
whose remote and immediate causes are traceable to ethnicity. By the end of this
chapter, students should be able to define ethnicity, distinguish between the four major
theoretical frameworks and analyze the root causes of communal conflicts in Nigeria
using specific case studies.
Ethnicity
Prior to the partition of Africa, the various ethnic nationalities, each with its own
internalroles,norms,andcohesiveness,coexistedandmaintaineda.chainofsocial and
economic interrelationships among them.Traditionally,African societies functioned
through an elaborate system based on the family, the lineage, the clan, the tribe, and
ultimately a confederation of groups, each with its ethnic, cultural, and linguistic
characteristics. These formed the units of social, economic, and political organizations
and inter-communal relations. The colonialists split up and arbitrarily brought them
19
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 17]
together without regard to their common ancestral characteristics or ascriptions.They
were placed in new administrative structures, governed by alien rules, values,
institutions,and principles,Thegroups losttheir independence and autonomy,having
beendivestedofthepowerandauthorityassociatedwithtraditional self-governance.
The centralization of power brought them underthe direct control of the alien
authoritarian colonial government with abstract laws and new ways of life. The
coercion of hitherto disparate groups into particular political entities with centralized
ofdominationandpossibleloss ofidentity.
By definition, an ethnic group is a community of people who believe that they possess
a common identity based on issues of origin, kinship ties, historical experiences,
traditions, cultures, and language. They are social formations which are distinguished
by their individual communal character (Okpala, 2025). Ethnicity as a social
phenomenon drives the social dynamics that traverse the entire spectrum of African
life, including human identity and social organization (Ojiezele & Ojo, 2024).
According to Nnoli (1978),ethnicityis a social phenomenon associated with
interactions among members of different ethnic groups. The inference is that ethnicity
is a situation in which individuals in a particular ethnic group consider themselves or
areconsideredbyotherstohavecommon affinity,whichdistinguishesthemfromother
groups in the society. People and their actions are judged or evaluated and understood
on the basis of the group to which they belong. It manifests in all aspects of one's life
as a member of an ethnic group - economic, social, psychological, political, etc. The
inferenceis that ethnicity isa dynamic and sociallyconstructed phenomenon thatdrives
individuals belonging to particular ethnic groups to identify themselves based on shared
cultural characteristics. The sense of communality affects the performance and
functioning of the African leaders because they are influenced in their actions and
decisions by ethnic loyalty (Nnoli, 1978).
Asanebi (2017) explained that the fierce struggle for resources among the African
ethnic groups was deliberately orchestrated by the colonialists, whose primary interest
was economic exploitation. According to him, they introduced the centrally controlled
resource governance system that divested the indigenes of the rights over such
endowments. In return, the colonial State provided skeletal welfare services in the form
of basic social amenities. The groups, having been divested of the ownership or control
of the natural resources, became increasingly dependent on what was provided by the
colonial State.The consequential dependency syndrome led the groups to conceive the
State as the provider of social amenities, and that access to and use of resources should
better serve the individual's group needs rather than those of the collective, It nurtured
cleavages along ethnic lines and a zero-sum or winner-takes-all attitude that underlies
the intractable struggle for access to resources.Today, African Nations are
characterized by ethnic entities that make varied and specific demands on the State.
The exit of the colonialists on independence further sharpened the competition and
conflict over the control of the State organs or structures and, consequently. the
20
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 18]
resources of the already fragmented nations.The interests do not include the need for
investments for the collective growth or common good of all. The struggle by the
groups is for control of government structures, including posts and positions, for the
appropriation and expropriation of public resources for the best interest of the dominant
group members (Asanebi, 2017).
As a tool, ethnicity worked well for the colonialists. It was strategically used to create
disharmonyamongthefederatingethnicgroupsthatmakeupthecontemporaryAfrican
States. It is observable that presently, the differences in size, cultural variations, and
other social dynamics of the constituent ethnic groups create antagonistic relationships
that tend towards disunity and conflict. According to Ebegbulem (201l), multi-ethnic
States are prone to conflict and competitive relationships as different groups struggle
to control the political power and economic resources ofthe state.Ethnicityprovides
the platform on which the individual groups mobilize to actualize their economic goals.
Egwu (2001) pointed out that ethnicity is characterized by exclusiveness and the
common consciousness of one's cultural superiority to others. It accentuates
competition by individuals and groups for scarce public resources such as government
contracts, employment, political appointments, scholarships, property rights,
opportunities for lucrative trade and commerce, etc.
According to Okpan & Otega (2019), the consequences of ethnicity are multifarious. It
breeds the monsters that have been entrenched in the psyche of Africans, which
undermine the collective quests for unity and development. Today, ethnicity manifests
in variousforms that include prebendal orethnicpolitics,nepotism,greed, corruption,
civil strife, bigotry, wars, genocide, deprivation, etc. Ethnicity is at the heart of
escalating incidences of violence such as insurgency, terrorism, banditry, herdsmen
predation, etc. Politics and religion are commonly used by the leaders to manipulate
the way ethnic group members behave towards each other.
MajorTheories of Ethnicity
Ethnicity is a multiplex concept that has been studied from various perspectives.The
major theories that have been proposed to explain ethnicity include Primordialism,
Instrumentalism, Social Constructivism and Ethno-symbolism (Ononogbu, 2017;
Smith, 2009).
Primordialism: The theory views ethnicity as a given, natural and inherent aspect of
individuals and societies and argues that ethnic identities are fixed at birth and
unchanging, often tied to factors such as ancestry, kinship, language, culture, history
and territory.Ethnicity is an innate and fundamental aspect of.human identity.and
ethnic identities are deeply rooted in history and are often tied to specific geographical
regions. According to the theory, ethnic conflicts are inevitable due to the deep-seated,
unchanging nature of ethnic identities.As objective reality,it is a fundamental part of
21
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 19]
Instrumentalism:Instrumentalism views ethnicity as a social construct that is
manipulated by individuals and groups for their own benefit. It argues that ethnic
identities are not fixed, but rather areflexible and can change over time. Ethnicity is
not an inherent human nature but is constructed and manipulated for political,
economic, or social gain.Ethnic identities can change over time and are often used as
tools to achieve certain goals.Ethnic conflicts are surmountable but they persist
because they are manipulated by elites or other powerful groups to keep the gullible
subordinatesdivided.
Social Constructivism: Social Constructivism views ethnicity as a social construct that
is fluid, created and maintained through social interactions and processes. It posits that
cthnic identities are neither fixed nor inherent, but rather are constructed and
reconstructed through social interactions. Ethnicity, as a social construct, is created and
maintained through social interactions. Therefore, ethnic identities are not biologically
fixed or inherent, but rather are constructed and reconstructed over time.Ethnic
conflicts are not inevitablebut are often the result of social processes and interactions.
Ethno-symbolism: The theory offers a slightly different perspective on the nature and
significance ofethnicity by emphasizing shared symbols, myths and traditions and their
roles in shaping ethnic identity (Smith, 2009). It argues that ethnicity is rooted in shared
cultural elements like history,language,rituals, etc., which provide meaning and
continuity to a group. The symbolic elements create a sense of belonging, provide a
shared narrative and legitimize group claims that explain the psychological and
emotional component of ethnicity. The groups first reify the myths and syinbols and
legitimize same by their claims to common historical antecedents. The ethnic symbols
provide the motive force that drives a sense of common historical experience and
descent, creating a feeling of unifying relationshipor national identitythat manifest as
ethnic nationalism.Ethno-symbolism provides the cultural raw materials on the basis
of whichethnicnationalismis built.
EthnicIdentityinAfrica
All African states,tosaytheleast,werevictimsofcolonialpower.Theywereterritories
whoseborders were drawn artificially at the BerlinConference in1885bythe colonial
powerdone in orderto align with colonial administrativeand economic interests.After
claiming power,the colonial overlords defined, classified, numbered and mapped
African ethnic groups inorderto createand solidifyadministrativeunitstofacilitatea
stronger political and institutional control(Young,2004).Forinstance,inNigeria,the
British colonial power forcefully amalgamated independent nations with different
cultures andwaysof lifetobecomeonenation-state.
Decentralized despotism under colonialism involved the use of traditional and local
chiefs through patronizing relationship where their loyalty was rewarded through
access to resources controlled by the colonial power.Ethnicity became an important
instrument to the colonial divide and rule device used for the purpose of political.
22
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 20]
cnforcement of taxes and extraction of wealth (Broch-Due. (2005).To further create
enmity among different cthnic formations, the colonial state drove a wedge between
cthnic groups by giving preferential treatment to some identity groups through
appointment of local authorities or administrative staff in the colonial offices. The
impact of these policies created new cleavage of class thus exacerbating existing
internal dfferences ofgender,tribalism,andethnic clientele.Power was given tosome
at the expense of others thus creating frustration and competition which served the
interest of the colonial power (Ekeh, 1975).
Colonialism continues to play some pivotal role in African conficts through some other
negative connotations such as neo-colonization, relative deprivation, subjugation, etc.
The phenomena serve as a lever used by politicians to mobilize ethnic support in pursuit
of power, wealth, and influence.In Africa, ethnic identity becomes an issue during
elections because politicians use them to mobilize support and influence.
Triggers of Ethnic Identity and Conflict in Africa
Often conflicts inAfrica havebeen attributedwithinthebroadercontextofcolonialism
and the crisisof the post-colonial state.Bythemid-1950s manyAfrican states have
gained political independence and freedom to handle their own affairs but development
has not beenpossibledueto neo-colonialism.Thecolonialmasters havecontinuedto
control the economy of their erstwhile colonies by manipulating the electoral process
to make sure that imperialist lackeys emerge as leaders.Thus, at the heart ofthe African
crisis is the failure of most African states to manage their identity in the process of
democratization andinstitution building.Politicization and mismanagement oftherich
ethnic African diversity have continued to be one of the causes of political crisis and is
often followed by ethnic wars and ethnicrivalry (Berman, 1998).
Since the mid-1960s, Africa has experienced protracted ethnic-related conflicts,
including but not limited to civil wars in states like Nigeria, Somalia, Rwanda, Darfur,
Sudan, Algeria, Burundi, Chad, Congo-Brazzaville, the Democratic Republic of Congo
(formerly Zaire), Cote d' Ivoire, Eritrea, Liberia, to name but a few. The Stockholm
International Peace Research Institute listed 12 high-intensity armed conflicts in sub-
Saharan Africa in 2021 alone (SIPRI, 2022). The Institute further outlined some notable
ethnic identity conflicts in Africa. In Nigeria the major ethnic groups namely Hausa-
Fulani, Igbo, and Yoruba clashed over resources, power, and regional autonomy,
notably in the Biafra War (1967-1970) and ongoing banditry and Islamic jihadists. Over
two million people died during the Biafra war, In Rwanda, the Hutu and Tutsi groups
were involved in the 1994 genocide, resulting in over 1 million deaths. In Sudan and
South Sudan, the Dinka, Nucr, and other groups fought over resources and power,
particularly in Darfur and South Sudan's civil war. In the Congo Democratic Republic
(DRC), the Luba, Lunda, Hema, and Lendu ethnic groups fought over resources like
diamonds and coltan. In Mali and Burkina Faso, the Fulani and Tuareg ethnic groups
face tensions and violence, often linked to jihadist groups and resource competition.
There are also Fulani herdsmen and farmer clashes in Ghana,Benin and Cote d'lvoire
23
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 21]
caused by conmpetition for resources, land degradation and climate change. In South
Africa,the Zulu, Xhosa and Afrikaner ethnic groups have experienced conflict from
the apartheid era and post-election violence. In each instance, the groups mobilize
along ethnic lines to compete for resources (SIPRI, 2022).
The general impression is that Africa is enmeshed in cyclic ethnic conflicts. The groups
nurse grievances, whether perceived or real, against each other which eventually serve
as the motivation or catalyst for reprisals. Some of the conflicts are centuries-old,
predating colonial rule, intractable, and defying resolution.The obvious implication is
that Africa's complicated ethnic diversity leaves the continent perpetually vulnerable
to devastating, intermittent conflict. The condition negates the prospects for sustained
economicgrowthanddevelopment.
On the contrary, most ethnic identity conflicts of the post-colonial era are self-serving.
Aapengnuo (2010) posited that ethnicity is typically not the driving force of African
conflicts but a lever used by politicians to mobilize supporters in pursuit of power,
wealth, and resources. It is agreeablethat ethnic groups are the predominant means of
social identity formation in Africa but the entities coexisted peacefully as aggregates
with a high degree of interrelationship through interethnic marriage, economic
partnerships, and shared values before the advent of colonialism. The recourse to ethnic
powerand resources,necessarilyfroman intrinsichatred.
In Rwanda, the Hutus and Tutsis have intermarried, share the same spoken language,
and faith. The ethnic identities were closely associated with their interchangeable
occupations, which are farmer or herder.Earlier skirmishes in pre-colonial Rwanda had
usually been over resources and power.However, the political manipulation of these
resource conflicts led to the well-orchestrated 1994 genocide. The politicians,
demagogues, and the media used ethnicity to mobilize popular sentiments to eliminate
political opponents. This snowballed into a planned campaign of mass murder in
Rwanda that occurred over the course of some 100 days in April-July 1994. The
genocide was conceived by extremist elements of Rwanda' s majority Hutu
population who planned to kill the minority Tutsi population and anyone who opposed
those genocidal intentions. It is estimated that some 200,o00 Hutu, spurred on by
propaganda from various media outlets, participated in the genocide. More than
800,000 civilians-primarily Tutsi, but also moderate Hutu-were killed during the
campaign.As many as 2,000,000 Rwandans fled the country during or immediately
after the genocide (Britannica, n.d.).
Nigeria presents evenamorecomplex scenario.Therehadbeen isolated religious crises
between the Christian Southerners who areresident in the predominantly Muslin north.
Presently, there are constant eruptions of violence against northern Christians by
Islamic jihadists especially in thenorth-west.There arealsothemaraudingbandits who
24
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 22]
are attacking,killingabducting and disposscssingbothnorthrnChristiansandnativ
HausaMuslimsoftheirproperties,including their ancestral lands.TheterroristIslamic
jihadists target schools and churches while also attacking and abducting non-Fulani
Moslems and Christians including men,women, and children for ransom.Both the
bandits and Islamic jihadist terrorists attack state institutions, including the security
agencies. In the Kanuri area of Nigeria's Northeast, the Federal government has been
fighting to the contain Boko Haram insurgency.The herder-farmer conflict involving
essentially the Fulani cattle-herders and local farmers is ravaging the highly diverse
middlebelt region and other parts of the country.The herder-farmerviolence is usually
reported as communal conflict because it is sustained by the indigenes or non-
indigenes/settlers'conundrum,
The question that arises is: How can Africans build unified nations with many
ethnicities living peacefully and coexisting? One of the steps is infrastructure
development and cconomic growth.These tools have shown to be effective in fostering
social harmony in places where poverty is atrigger.of ethnic tensions.Also,a strong
state where corruption is eliminated can transform cthnicity froma negative force into
a positive one with democracy as a superstructure (Call, 2003). Unfortunately,
democracy inAfrica has been manipulated bythose who crave for power.This is why
democracymeans muchmorethanelections.Minority ethnicgroups can betaken over
or swallowed by dominant ethnic groups.
Democracy can thrive and be a portent force to mitigate conflict and where there is
government by the people and where citizens' rights, duties and representation are
honored.Democracy as remedy for social conflicts in Africa also means independent
courts,robust institutions,strongcivil societyparticipation,ruleoflaw,propertyrighs,
free press and especiallytolerance and open space for minorities.The mismanagement
of the richness of ethnic diversity is oflen linked to the absence of visionary and
nationalist leaders.African States need institutions and structures that reflect ethnic
diversity and respect for minority rights, power-sharing,and checks and balances to
reduce the perception of injustice and insccurity that facilitate cthnic conflicts.
Types of Ethnic Identity Conflict
Most often,identity conflicts do not show themselves clearly.It may be couched or
manifested as cthnic solidarity with a tint of religious coloration and regional
autonomy.Each type has different drivers, escalation patterns,and demands different
interventions. According to Okonkwo (2025),approaching a conflict situation with the
wrongdiagnosis willdefinitely lead to disastrous outcomes.He outlined threetypes of
cthnic identity conflict whicharebrieflyexplainedbelow:
Ethnic Conflicts-These are conflicts thatcentre on ancestry,kinship,and heredityor
perceived blood ties. They involve groups that define membership through descent
ratherthan choicc.The Hutu-Tutsi violence in Rwanda is a typical exampleof ethnic
conflict. The same thing applies to the Fulani-farmer crisis in Nigeria, Mali, and
Burkina Faso. Bclonging to an ethnic group is acquired at birth, learned through
25
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 23]
socialization, and transmitted across generations.Their historical narratives hinge on
common ancestral origins, symbols, and territorial claims. Violent conficts often target
all members ofthe group instead of specific individuals.
Religious Conflicts-Religion is a set of beliefs,practices,and rituals centered or a
higher power or spiritual force. It is an integral part of culture that confers identity,
unifies, and mobilizes against out-group meimbers.Religious conflicts mobilize
believers around faith, doctrine, and divine mandate. Unlike ethnic identity, religious
affiliation permits conversion,and-membership may traverse ethnic groups.For
example, the ethnic Kanuri dominate the leadership of Boko Haram, but the sect
transcends ethnicboundaries.It embraces all who accept its ideologyand interpretation
of Islamicdoctrines,while itsmembership cuts across ethnic lines.
Territorial or Regional Conflicts -Territorial conflicts revolve around the identity
conferredonagroupbyvirtueoftheirgeographic location inrelation tothegovernance
arrangements. The regions struggle against each other and against the central
governments over access to resources.Membership derives from location rather than
ancestryor belief.Anyone living withintheterritorycanrightfully claimbelonging.In
South Cameroon,the members of the Ambazonia movement are Anglophones from
diverse ethnic backgrounds that are united around shared regional grievances. Their
territorial identities centre on their distinct colonial history -they are governed by the
English common law and speak English language. In Nigeria, the North-South
dichotomy,the geopolitical zones arrangement, and the inherent conflicts associated
with them areexamples ofregional conflicts.
Irobi(2005)alsoobserved that ethnic identity conflicts can manifest in thefollowing
forms but that the categories are not mutually exclusive as they often overlap, and so
involvemultiplecauses.
Ethno-nationalist conflicts-when a groupdesiresfor self-deternination,autonomy,or
independence e.g. separatist movements.
Ethnic rivalry conflicts -competition between groups for resources, power, or status
e.g. Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba vs. Igbo.
Ethno-religious conflicts -tensions betiween groups with different religious affiliations
(e.g., Christians vs. Muslims in some African countries.
Resource-based conflicts - disputes over land, water, or other resources e.g.farmer-
herder conflicts in Nigeria.
Identity-based conflicts - conflicts centered on issues of identity, culture, or historical
grievances e.g., Hutu vs.Tutsi in Rwanda.
Causes of Ethnic Identity Conflict
As earlier indicated, ethnic identity conflicts in Africa are caused by many factors that
often combine in disproportionate forins that are sometimes difficult to identify.The
sources of the conflicts are commonly classified and attributed to social, economic.
political or religious factors. It is however, necessary to understand how the factors
26
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 24]
interplay or combine lo produce the complex wcb of devastating conflicts. In this
regard, Jibat (2024) explored some of the factors that cause conflict in Africa
EconomicFaclors-Thecompetitionforscarceresourcesisacommonfactorinalmost
all ethnic conflicts in Africa. The multi-ethnic nature ofAfrican States, underlined by
mutual suspicion and mistrust, pits the ethnic communities violently against each other
in the competition for resources e.g. property rights, jobs, education, identity, health
care,andothersocialamenities.
Psychological Factors -Another major cause of ethnic conflict is the psychological
disposition of the members. The competing ethnic groups, given the fact that they are
not equal in size and social capital, are fearful ofbeing dominated bythe more powerful
groups or of the obliteration of their identity. Fear of domination might include the
possible denial of access to resources indispensable to the group's survival. In some
instances, ethnic bigots and extremists build upon such fears to polarize the society.
The traumas of the Rwandan genocide, the Sudanese, Biafran, etc., magnify these
anxieties.
Absence of strong social institutions - African nations lack strong institutions.
Institutions are the established, enduring patterns of rules, roles, and relationships that
prescribe how a society is organized to meet its basic needs. Institutions provide the
blueprint on the basis of which societies are governed. The existing institutions
engender ethnic conflicts, which account for the inability of the constituent ethnic
groups to overcome their primordial propensities. The relative deprivation of groups
undermines the effectiveness of good governance; especially its ability to address
accountability and transparency makes it possible for corrupt public officials to go
unpunished.
Colonial legacy - Colonial powers drew borders that lumped different ethnic groups
together, while favoring some groups over others. For example, Belgium favored Tutsis
over Hutus in Rwanda, while the British colonialists introduced direct and indirect rules
in Nigeria.
Political manipulation - Ethnic conflicts are fundamentally political conflicts, driven
by non-inclusive political systems, monopolization of state resources, and
manipulation of ethnicityfor political gain.Poor governance and elite misuse of power
are more fundamental causes than resource competition or ethnic diversity.Ethnicity
SelectedConflictCasesinNigeria
The history of Nigeria is replete with cases of inter-ethnic, inter-communal, inter-
religious and inter-personal, etc. forms of conflicts. Virtually all communities at one
time or the other experience clashes that have degenerated to huge-loss of lives and
properties, injuries inflicted on people and displacement of inhabitants. One of the
major factors found to be at thecentre ofmost conflicts in Nigeria is Communal fand.
Communal conflicts are violent or nonviolent confrontations between groups that
define themselves along shared identity lines. Often times the conflict concerns claims
or accusations of trespasses overtheothercommunity's land eitherforfarmworkor
27

[Page 25]
the exploitation'of mineral resources. Also conflicts between families may result in
killings or destruction of properties. Inter-communal conflicts may be caused by
improper sharing or non-availability of basic amenities like portable water, roads,
electricity, schools where one community prevents others from benefitting from the
amenities (Allen, et al, 20i9). Typical examples of land-related conflicts include
Aguleri-Umuleri, Zangon-Kataf, Ife-Modakeke, Izzi and Ezza, Ikwo and Izzi, etc. This
section examines some individual cases highlighting the actors, understanding the
remote and immediate causes and the intervention strategies.
I. Aguleri - Umuleri Land Dispute
At the centre ofthe conflict betiween Aguleri and Umueri was Otuocha - a beach on the
eastern part of the Omambala (Anambra) River, which is a tributary of the River Niger.
The land stretches about 92 metres inland; and bounded on the north east by Emu
stream, a tributary ofOmambala River; on the south east and south west, by Akor River,
another tributary of Omambala River. Otuocha became a popular port of call for
European missionaries and people from the Igbo hinterland in the nineteenth century.
It is on record that Aguleri community, through Eze IdigoI (the reigning king) and
some elders granted a portion of land at Otuocha to the Royal Niger company on the
7th of September, 1891 (Ekeh, 2011).
Consequently, Umuleri chiefs led by the Umuchezi discovering the gains'of lease of
lands to Europeans sold a portion ofthe Otuocha land also to the Royal Niger Company
on 4th January, 1898. Leases were entered into between the two communities, and
different European groups, over portion of Otuocha land, and these beneficiaries
include the Church Missionary Society (CMS) (1920) for the purpose of erecting a
church building, John Holt Group (1916), and CFAO) in (1931). The contention
between Aguleri and Umuleri over the exclusive ownership of Otuocha, where both
communities inhabit, took them through series of litigations and fratricidal
bloodletting.
It does appear that the conflicts between the two Communities predate the arrival of
the Europeans and the argument centers on which of the groups settled first and had
prior ownership of Otuocha. Eri factor in the historical origin of Aguleri and Umuleri
communities is another central factor in the conflicts between the duo (Ifediora, 1996).
The struggle over the ownership of Otuocha land took the Aguleri and Umuleri
communities through litigations in courts of competent jurisdiction, both within and
outside the shores ofNigeria.Court actions were instituted by the two communities in
the Native Courts, West African Court of Appeal (WACA), and the Privy Council in
London. After Nigeria's Independence in 1960, the cases were also adjudicated on at
the Onitsha and Otuocha High Courts respectively, the Federal Court of Appeal, and
terminated at the Supreme Court of Nigeria in 1984.The first court action instituted
over the Otuocha land was in 1920 at the instance of the Umuleri community.

A variety of Intervcntion strategies were applied in the Aguleri-Umuleri communal

(a). Government and Legal Interventions;
I4-Member Peace Panel: The state government set up panels to establish the

oathstopreventfurtherhostilities.

hold legitimacy, to negotiate peace.

Community Mediation - Bringing together community leaders to discuss,
share perspectives, and renegotiate boundaries.

Peace Education through the Introduction of culturally sensitive education that

Youth engagement and reorientation focusing on youth empowerment and

Encouraging social Communication by building social networks like social

thetwogroups.

II.Ife-Modakeke Crisis
The status of Modakeke and that of its people have always been a source ofdispute and
conflictdueto issuesrelatingto landlord/tenant relationshipor indigene/non-indigene
issues (Oladoyin, 2001). Ife people who are the original settlers in the area insist that
migrated and settled on the land as far back as i7th century as a result of the collapse
of old Oyo empire. In both Ife and Modakeke, ethnic attachment is high and
interpersonal relationship among the people of the two towns is not very cordial.
Some of the later conflicts between the two communities include conflict over the
establishment of Modakeke High School, conflict overthe-establishment-of
Olorunsogo plank market, opposition to self-help development projects by a fund-
raising activity of Modakekein1980.The requestfor a separateLocal Government
Council which began since the1950s was perceived as an attempt at self-determination
and culminated in serious violent crisis between Ife and Modakekebetween2000and
29
Scanned with

[Page 27]
2001.The conflicf claimed several lives and properties including the destruction of
farms and settlements worth millions ofNaira (Babajimi,2003).
MajorCausesof fe-Modakeke Crisis
The major identified causes and triggers ofthe Ife-Modakeke crises include:
i.Land disputes:Amajor and persistent cause of conflict had been disagreements
over land ownership and rights,with Ife people viewing themselves as
landownersandModakekeastenants.
i. Sovereignty and identity: The Modakeke people have sought a greater sense of
sovereignty and a distinct identity, which has clashed with the Ife people's
perception of their historical authority (Bajo, 2014).
ili. Local government creation: The creation and location of the headquarters of the
Ife-East Local Government Area in 1997 ignited a major conflict. The Ife
indigenes wanted the headquarters located in a predominantly Ife area, while
Modakeke people felt politically marginalized and demanded their own
headquarters.
iv. Historical and cultural factors: The historical tension is rooted in the 19th-
century displacement of the Oyo people and their settlement in the area, which
created a basis for the ongoing conflict over land rights and status.
v.Other causes include social and economic tensions, political representation, and
even cultural differences, such as religious or symbolic disputes, for example
the crossing of masquerades.
Intervention Stralegies:
The Ife-Modakeke crisis remains one of Nigeria's longest-running intra-ethnic
conflicts. The major causes of the protracted conflict are identified as land/tenancy
disputes, competition over local government authority, boundary disagreements, and
tomanagetheconflict.
(a). Formal peace-building strategies -negotiation, mediation, arbitration, dialogue
andrestorative justice.
(b). Government-led interventions
i. Deployment of security men during flare-ups (e.g, 1981, 1997-98, and 2000)
to restoreorderafterdestruction of homes and displacement.
i. Administrative restructuring: In I997, General Sani Abacha created Ife East
Local Government Area out of Ife North and Ife Central to address Modakeke
demands for their own Local Government Area.The dispute over where the
headquarters would be sited (Oke-Ogbo vs.a Modakeke area) reignited
violence.
ili.High-level peace committees:President Olusegun Obasanjo setuptheOlabode
George-led committeetoinvestigateandmediate.
(c). Traditional institutions
i.Traditional rulers and chiefs were constantly involved.
ii.Joint committees of chiefs from both parties met at intervals to discuss peace
andreach conclusions on salient issues.
(d).Community and socio-economic integration strategies (peace education)

[Page 28]
Since2000,relativepeace has been sustained less byformaltreaties andmore
byeverydaycoexistencethroughtoleranceas aconscious community norm.
i.Intermarriages between Ife and Modakeke families, creating kinship ties that
discouragerenewedviolence.
ili. Economic interdependence - shared markets, roads, schools and livelihoods
have made separation costlyand cooperation practical.
(e).Post-conflict peace-building programs
Training and re-orientation of law enforcement agencies.

ratherthan politicizingidentity
