[Page 65]
The Internet of Things (loT) and digital threat to peace and sccurity
Digital technology, being the technology that uses data to process or transmit digital
information has become central in people's daily lives. Gadgets like computers,
smartphones, apps, and Al tools run on digital technology. Digital technology is the
backbone of Internet of Things (loT). The concept of the Internet of Things (loT)
represents a transformative shift on how humans interact and relate with technology
and the physical environment.By definition, loT refers to a network of interconnected
devices embedded with sensors, sofiware, and communication capabilities that cnable
them to collect and exchange data over the internet (Ashton, 2009; Atzori, lera, &
Morabito, 2010).
An IoT platform collects data from its environment, either in a central or decentralized
manner. This data is transmitted over networks to platforms or other systems and
analyzed. Based on the results, actions are triggered such as turning on a device or
issuing an alert.A common example is smart thermostat that automatically adjusts to
room temperature. Other IoT devices includes wearable fitness trackers, sensors,
survelliance cameras, complex industrial machine components, and connected vehicles
thatwork togetherto enhance efficiency,convenience,and decision-making processes.
By bridging the gap between the digital and physical worlds, loT is fundamentally
reshapingmodern society.
In the last few years, the rapid evolution of information and communication
technologies has further fueled the development and growth of IoT, making it one of
themost important aspects of digital transformation indifferent industries.Industries
like healthcare, agriculture, transportation, and manufacturing are increasingly
adopting IoT technologies to enhance productivity, reduce operational costs, and
introduce innovative services in the marketplace (Manyika et al., 2015; Gubbi et al.,
2013). For 'example, smart healthcare devices help to monitor patients, while smart
agricultural devices help farmers to optimize crop production through data analysis.
These examples highlight how loT is not only connecting devices, but also creating
smarterenvironmentsand systems.
The evolution of IoT
The Internet of Things has evolved into a keytechnology in everyday life and industrial
processes. The history of loT began in the 1980s with the first ideas for connecting
physical objects. The concept was first articulated by Mark Weiser in the 1990s, who
envisioneda world in which technologybecomes seamlesslyintegrated intodaily life
(Weiser,1991).However,theterm"Internetof Things"was later coined byKevin
Ashton in 1999 to describe a system where physical objects are connected to the
internet through sensors and can exchange data without human intervention(Ashton,
2009).
In its earliest stage, IoT was limited by technological constraints, such as low
processing power, high costs, and limited internet accessibility (Zikria et. al., 2021).
73
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 66]
The early 2000s marked a significant turning point in the development of loT, driven
by advancements in wireless communication, sensor technologies, and internet
infrastructure. During this period, technologies such as Radio Frequency Identification
(RFID) played a key role in enabling objects to be uniquely identified and tracked
(Want, 2006). At the same time, the expansion of broadband internet and the increasing
adoption of mobile devices created a more conducive environment for interconnected
systems. These developments laid the foundation for machine-to-machine (M2M)
communication, which is a precursor to modern loT systems (Gubbi et al., 2013).
By the 2010s, loT experienced rapid growth due to the convergence of cloud
computing, big data analytics, and improved hardware capabilities. Devices became
more affordable, energy-efficient, and capable of processing large volumes of data in
real-time.This era saw the emergence ofsmart homes, wearable devices, and industrial
IoT applications, transforming sectors such as healthcare, agriculture, transportation,
and manufacturing (Atzori, Iera, & Morabito, 2010). Furthermore, the proliferation of
smartphones and mobile applications enhanced user interaction with IoT devices,
making the technology more accessible to the general population.
In recent years, the evolution of IoT has continued with the integration of emerging
technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), edge computing, and 5G networks.
These advancements have significantly improved the speed, efficiency, and intelligence
of IoT systems, enabling real-time decision-making and automation on a large scale
(Zanella et al., 2014). Today, loT is a critical component of digital transformation,
contributing to the development of smart cities and intelligent systems. As the
technology continues to evolve, challenges such as data security, privacy, and inter-
operability remain important areas of concernthatmust beaddressed to fully realize
thepotentialofIoT.
Applications of IoT in everydaylife
The applications of IoT are vast and continue to expand as technology evolves. One of
the most visible applications is in smart homes, where connected devices allow users
to control lighting, heating, security systems, and appliances remotely. These systems
resource usage.For example, smart thermostats can automatically adjust temperature
settings based on user behavior, reducing energy consumption.
In healthcare, loT has revolutionized patient care by cnabling remote monitoring and
telemedicine. Telemedicine is the use of digital communication tools, such as video
calls, phone calls, or apps - to provide healthcare services remotely instead of in-
person.Wearable devices such as fitness trackers and smartwatches can monitor vital
signs,includingheartrate,physicalactivity,andsleep patterns.Thisdata canbe shared
with healthcare providers, allowing for early detection of health issues and timely
intervention (Manyika et al., 2015). loT also supports the management of chronic
diseases by providing continuous monitoring and personalized treatment plans,
74
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 67]
The agricultural sector has also benefited significantly from loT technologies.Smart
farming techniques use sensors and data analytics to monitor soil moisture, weather
conditions,and crop health.This information helps farmers makeinformed decisions
about irrigation, fertilization, and pest control, leading to increased productivity and
sustainability.Similarly,loTis transformingtransportation throughthedevelopmentof
smart cities. Connectedvehicles, traffic management systems, and intelligent
infrastructure work together to reduce congestion, improve safety, and enhance the
overall efficiency of transportation systems (Gubbi et al., 2013).
BenefitsoftheInternetofThingsiu
The widespreadadoptionof IoToffers numerousbenefits acrossdifferentsectors.One
of the most significant advantages is increased efficiency and productivity.By
automating routine tasks and enabling real-time monitoring, loT reduces the need for
human intervention and minimizes errors.In industrial settings,IoT systems can
monitor cquipment performance and predict maintenance needs, thereby reducing
downtime and improving operationalefficiency (Manyika et al., 2015).
Another important benefit of IoT is improved decision-making. The data generated by
IoT devices provides valuable insights that organizations can use to make informed
decisions.For example, businesses can analyze customer behavior to improve products
and services, while governments can use IoT data to enhance public services and
infrastructure. This data-driven approach leads to better planning, resource allocation,
and overall performance.
IoT also promotes innovation and economic growth. By enabling new business models
and services, IoT creates opportunities for entrepreneurs and organizations to develop
innovative solutions.For instance, smart energy systems allow consumers to monitor
and manage their energy usage, leading to cost savings and environmental
sustainability. As IoT continues to evolve, its potential to drive economic development
and improvequalityof lifebecomes increasinglyevident.
Internet of Things (loT) as a digital threat to peace and security
The Internet of Things (loT)refers toa rapidly expanding network of interconnected
devices, such as smart home systems, industrial sensors, medical devices,and critical
infrastructure controls that communicate and exchange data over the internet.While
loTenhancesefficiency,automation,andreal-timedecision-making,italsointroduces
significant digital vulnerabilities that can threaten peace and security at individual,
national, and global levels.
A major concern is the increased attack surface created by billions of connected
devices, many of which lack strong security protections.These vulnerabilities can be
exploited by cybercriminals or hostile actors to gain unauthorized access, disrupt
systems, or steal sensitive data. In critical sectors. such as energy, healthcare, and
75
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 68]
transportation, compromised IoT systems can lead to service disruptions, physical
damage, or even loss of life, thereby posing serious risks to national security.
IoT devices are also frequently used in large-scale cyberattacks, such as Distributed
Denial ofService(DDoS)attacks,wherecompromiseddevicesarecontrolledremotely
to overwhelm networks and disable services.Additionally,the extensive data collection
by IoT systems raises concerns about privacy violations and mass surveillance,as
sensitive personal and organizational information can be intercepted or misused.
Furthermore, the rapid growth of IoT often outpaces regulatory frameworks and
security standards, creating governance gaps that increase exposure to cyber threats.
These risks are compounded bythe integration of loT with other emerging technologies
like Artificial Intelligence, which can amplify both the scale and sophistication of
attacks.
Operationally, when IoT systems are compromised, attackers can take control of
devices that manage real-world operations, leading to serious consequences. The
consequences canbecategorized into:
Service disruptions: Many essential services like electricity (smart grids),
water supply,transportation,and hospital systemsdepend on IoT.If hacked,
these systems can be shut down or overloaded, causing blackouts, traffic chaos,
orhospitalfailures.
Physical damage: IoT controls machines in industries and infrastructure.
Attackers can manipulate settings (e.g.,pressure in pipelines, temperature in
factories),leading toequipmentfailure,explosions,ordestruction ofassets.
Loss of life: In critical sectors like healthcare and transportation,compromised
IoT devices (e.g.,connectedmedical equipment ortraffic control systems)can
malfunction, delay emergency responses, or cause accidents, putting lives at
risk.
Policyand peacebuildingrecommendations
To reduce digital threats to peace and security,several policy measures are necessary:
1.Cyber norms and global governance:International institutions must establish
norms regulating cyberwarfare,Al weapons,anddigital interference.
2. Peace-centered tech design: Technology developers should integrate conflict
sensitivity and human rights safeguards into digital systems.
3. Digital literacy for peace: Citizens need education on misinformation detection,
online dialogue ethics, and cyber resilience.
4. Inclusive access: Reducing digital inequality is necessary to prevent structural
violenceandexclusion.
5. Human oversight: AI in security contexts must remain under meaningful human
control.
76
Scanned with
CSCamScanner

[Page 69]
Above a, government and relevant stakeholders should prioritize the development of
indigenous technologies and promote technological selfreliance in Nigeria and Africa.
technological innovations would enhance national sovereignty, strengthen
cybersecurity, improve data protection, and reduce dependence on foreign-owned
technologies. Curently, most digital technologies, network infrastructure, sofware
commerce, and digital communication vulnerabie to external control and survellance.
Developing local technological capacity would reduce these security risks, protect
national intelligence and sensitive data, and ensure the stability and sustainability of
Nigeria's digital economy. These recommendations align with the preventive
peacebuilding approach central to Peace and Conflict Studies.
Conclusion
Technology and digital systems have fundamentally altered the meaning of conflict,
violence, and peace. Cyber warfare, misinformation, surveillance, Biotechnology,
Internet of Things and artificial intelligence now shape the security environment in
ways that traditional peace theories alone cannot fully explain. Yet, these same tools
also hold transformative potential for peacebuilding, dialogue, and conflict prevention.
For Peace and Conflict Studies as a discipline, the challenge is not simply to condemn
technology, but to critically examine its dual role as both a source of insecurity and an
instrument forpeace,

C. J. Ugwokel C, R. Nnamdi-Chlawal C, C. Onah] S. O, Kalul O, E, Oril I, J. Eze
Introductlon.
Womenfolk across cultures, time, and space have been subjected to varying degrees of
ill-treatment in one way or another, Thus, women suffer significantly due to their
gender (Ojemeiri, Aondover, and Aruaye 2022).The challenges faced by the women
basically because of their gender spring from the wrong perceptions, false narratives,
misrepresentations, and misinterpretations of their gender by society, both in the past
and present, Therefore, every society across cultures has male-dominated narratives of
patriarchy, The patriarchal narrative of society by men shapes and influences roles,
rights, liberties, access to power, decisions, inheritance, status, possession, etc., thereby
giving men undue advantages over women in so many spheres of life and socicty.
Evidently, the female gender, especially in Africa, and Nigeria in particular, has been
grossly maltreated and at times unjustly silenced based on social misconception of the
female gender or sex disposition.The maltreatment of women creates conflict in
society, It leads to the concept of gender-based violence, Gender-based violence is a
kind of conflict that arises from deprivation, subjugation, denial of rights, unjust
treatments,and punishments, among others, inflicted on a person or a people, basically
because oftheir gender,Gender-based violence could be directed against boys/men or
girls/women, However,girls/women suffer gender-based violence more than
boys/men.This isduetothepatriarehal narrative,misperception and misrepresentation
of society.Therefore, patriarchy, according to Nwano and Akhirome-Omonfuegbe
(2024), is one ofthe greatest setbacks to women's rights enforcement and protection in
Nigeria.
Right from the era of primitive society to the current globalized age, evidence abounds
that women have always been faced with social, cultural, religious, marital, economic,
sexual, educational,health, emotional,political,and physical violence inflicted against
them with impunity in varying degrees across the globe. People across cultures, space,
and time have their unique sorrows unleashed against their womenfolk -daughters,
girls,sisters,wives,and mothers.Emezi and Chris(2017)corroboratethat all societies
demonstrate characteristies of male superiority that are firmly rooted in the structural
composition of patriarchal ideology in socio-cultural activities. This confers
unnecessary advantages to boys over girls, Hence, gender-based violence in most
societies is structured violence because it is built into the specific patterns upon which
societies operate, Gender-based violence occurs mainly in the religions and cultures of
differentpeoples,
Gender based violence is rooted in the deprivation of the rights of women. This is
traceable to long-established man-made order (patriarchal structures in forms of

CSCamScanner

[Page 71]
institutions and roles),inqualitiesfoisted insocietyandmolywith impunityagain
womenfolkbythe menfolk.Ofientimes,violenceagainstwomen isperpetratedbymen
in the expression of their self-acclaimed superiority and protection of their ego and
interests, Examples of the common gender-based violence against womanhood are
such as sexual violence likerape, Female Genital Mutilation (FGM),forcefullygiving
out under aged girls into marriages, beating and lacerating maidservants, subjecting
female children to doing heavy chores at homes while the boys play.around, female
teenagers thrown into the markets and streets to hawk during school hours instead of
going to school, and.conscious denial of education to the girl child in preference to
education of the boy child, among others.
Addressing GBV requires more than legal cnforcement; it demands holistic
interventions that tackle structural inequities, cultural norms, and socio-cconomic
vulnerabilities. Approaches that are survivor-led, community-centered, and
transformative provide meaningful opportunitiesforhealing,justice,and social change.
Furthermore, sustainable peace and gender equality dependon adequatefunding, local
participation, and frameworks that integrate gender perspectives in decision-making
processes. Subsequently, international instruments such as United Nations Security
Council Resolution 1325, the Beijing Platform for Action (1995), and the 1993
Declaration on the Elimination of Violence Against Women advocate for survivor-led
community-based, restorative, and adequately resourced strategies to address GBV,
challenge structural inequalities, and promote sustainable pcace and gender equity
More importantly,these approaches underscore the importance of women's meaningful
engagement in peace processes,
Conceptual Clarifications
Peace
"Peace" comes from the Latin word pax, primarily interpreted as a pact, a contract, or
an agreement to end war or any dispute or conflict between two people, nations, or
beyond the mere absence of war, encompassing justice, law, order, and effective
governance. Ibeanu (2006) conceptualises peace as a condition characterized by the
absence of social conflict and an enabling environment in which individuals and groups
can pursue and fulfil their needs and expectations. The term "peaceful" is commonly
used to describe a nation or region during periods marked by the absence of armed
conflict and violence (Dede, 2025). However, peace scholars have long distinguished
between two orders of peace. The Norwegian sociologist Johan Galtung introduced the
foundational distinction between negative peace, the mere absence of direct, organised
violence, and positive peace, which encompasses social justice, equitable institutions,
and the conditions that enable human flourishing (Galtung, 1969). Negative peace is
precarious and often temporary; positive peace addresses the structural inequalities and
injustices that generate durable, transformative conflict.
80

[Page 72]
The United Nations Charter, signed in 1946, articulated the international community's
discriminationand injustice areall potentialdrivers ofviolence,and addressingthem
is therefore foundational to any genuine-peace (UN Peacebuilding Support Office,
2024).Critically,eacethat isbuilt without thefuli participationowomnand without
addressing gender-based violence and inequality is structurally incomplete.
Gender
The concept of gender is usualy and incorectly used interchangeably with sex, While
sex refers to the biological and physiologicai characteristics that define males and

Special Adviser on Gender Issues (OSAGI), " gender "refers to the social ttributes and
opportunities associated with being male and female and the relationship between
women and men and girls and boys, as well as the relations between women and those
between men (UN OSAGI, 2001). These attributes and opportunities are not
biologically determined but socially constructed, learned through socialisation, and
subject to change over time and across cultural contexts. The terim "gender" denotes
"the socially constructed roles'and responsibilities deemed suitable for men and
women" (Peace Corps, 2020). Gender defines what is expected, permitted, and valued
in a woman or a man within a given social context. It shapes access to resources, the
division of labour, patterns of authority and subordination, and even the experience of
violence. The World Health Organisation (2023) defines gender as 'the characteristics
of women, men, girls and boys that are socially constructed, emphasising that gender
intersects with social and economic inequalities through the framework of
intersectionality. This intersectionality implies that gender is relational: it cannot be
understood in isolation but only in the context ofthe dynamic relationships among men,
women, boys, girls, and others whose identities do not conform to binary norms. An
intersectional approach 'to gender further recognises that gender is experienced
differently across other social markers such as class, race, ethnicity, age, religion, and
disability, producing layered and complex forms of inequality (Crenshaw, 1989; UN

Conflict resolution refers to a range of methods and processes by which parties to a

broader concept that aims to change the very nature of the relationships and social

2022). Within the UN system, conflict resolution is understood to encompass
preventive. diplomacy, mediation, , peacekeeping, peace enforcement, and
peacebuilding, each representing a different stage and modality of engagement (UN
Peacekeeping, 2024). Conflict resolution is the process of finding a peaceful and
acceptable solution to a disagreement between two or more people, groups, or nations.
It involves a series of steps, methods, and tools that help people in conflict talk through
their differences, understand each other, and agree on a way forward without resorting
to violence or prolonged hostility.
The common processes inelude: Negotiation: the parties talk directly to reach an
agreement. Mediation: a neutral third party helps the conflicting parties communicate
and reach a solution. Arbitration: a neutral party hears both sides and issues a binding
decision--reconciliation; rebuilding trust and relationships after a conflict. The

Historical Legacles and Gender-Based Violence in Sub-Saharan Africa
The persistence of gender-based violence (GBV) in Sub-Saharan Africa cannot be fully
understood without situating it within the region's historical trajectories, which have
shaped contemporary gender relations and social norms, Pre-colonial African societies

1986),. Feminist theoretical perspectives helpilluminate this dynamic, as the existence
of patriarchal hierarchies, even in pre-colonial contexts, provided a structural basis for
the subordination of women and the regulation of female behavior (Walby, 1990).
Colonialism significantly reshaped gender relations, reinforcing male dominance while
disrupting pre-existing social systems. European colonial administrations introduced
legal and economic systems that often marginalized women by restricting land
ownership, formal employment, and access to education (Amadiume, i987;
Nnaemeka, 2005). Missionary influence and Christian norms frequently replaced local
gender norms with Western patriarchal ideals, diminishing women's political and
economic authority (Parpart, 1989). Social learning theory can help explain how these
colonial interventions normalized hierarchical gender relations, as successive
generations internalized new power structures that privileged men and sanctioned
women's subordination (Bandura, 1977). Moreover, the colonial economy's emphasis
on cash crops and labor migration disrupted family and community networks, reducing
the social mechanisms that previously regulated conflict and curtailed violence against
women (Parpart, 1989). These structural changes not only increased women's
economic dependence on men but also created social environments where domestic
and sexual violence could occur with reduced accountability.
Post-colonial governance inherited these gendered inequities, resulting in legal and
institutional frameworks that often failed to protect women adequately. Customary law,
which continues to influence rural and peri-urban areas, frequently enforces male
authority in marriage, inheritance, and domestic relations, thereby institutionalizing
conditions that facilitate GBV (Merry, 2006; Tamale, 2000). Despite the adoption of
formal legal protections, enforcement remains inconsistent, especially in contexts
where traditional norms and local authorities retain significant influence. From a
human rights perspective, this gap reflects a disjunction between formal state
obligations and localized social practices, highlighting the need for contextually
sensitive policy interventions (United Nations, 1993).

women, reflecting the compounded effects of historical marginalization.
Understanding historical legacies is not only essential for theoretical analysis but also
has practical implications for policy and intervention. Recognizing that contemporary
GBV is rooted in pre-colonial structures, colonial disruptions, and post-colonial legal
and cultural continuities underscores the need for interventions that are multi-level,
context-sensitive, and historically informed.
Theoretical Perspectives on Understanding Gender-Based Violence
Gender-based violence (GBV) remains a persistent global problem, with profound
social, economic, psychological, and health consequences for individuals and societies.
Understanding its root causes, manifestations, and persistence requires a multifaceted
theoretical approach. Scholars have developed several perspectives--ranging from
feminist, social learning, ecological, power and control, cultural, conflict,
psychological, to human rights frameworks--to explain the dynamics of GBV. Each
theory provides a distinct lens, lluminating specific factors, yet no single theory offers
a comprehensive explanation. This section critically examines these theories, their
contributions, limitations, and gaps, thereby providing a foundation for a more
integrated understanding ofGBV.
Feminist Theory
Feminist theory has been central to scholarly discussions on GBV, emphasizing the
structural underpinnings of violence within patriarchal societies. Dobash and Dobash
(1979) argued that violence against women is not merely an individual phenomenon
but a mechanism through which men maintain dominance over women ini social,
84

[Page 76]
political, and domestic spheres. Walby (1990) further theorized that patriarchy operates
through multiple structures--including the household, culture, paid work, sexuality,
and the state--ensuring male authority is sustained across different domains of life.
Connell (2005) expanded this argument through the concept ofhegemonic masculinity,
demonstrating that dominant forms of masculinity legitimize aggression and control as
understanding structural inequality, scholars such as Heise (1998) and Jewkes (2002)
caution that an exclusive focus on patriarchy may overlook other significant factors,
including economic deprivation, cultural norms, and individual behavioral paterns.
Social Learning Thcory
Complementing the structural perspective, social learning theory providesinsight into
the behavioral transmission of violence. Bandura (1977) proposed that behavior,
including violent behavior, is learned through observation, imitation, and
reinforcement. Individuals exposed to violent models, particularly during childhood,
internalize such behaviors as acceptable responses to conflict. Jewkes (2002) observed
that exposure to domestic violence during formative years significantly increases the
likelihood of becoming a perpetrator or a victim in adulthood, demonstrating the
intergenerational nature of GBV. Social learning theory underscores the importance of
early interventions, educational programs, and media campaigns that model non-
violentbehaviors.
Ecological Theory
Ecological theory further expands the analysis by situating GBV within multi-level
contexts, recognizing that violence emerges from the interaction of individual,
relational, community, and societal factors (Bronfenbrenner, 1979; Heise, 1998).
Individual vulnerabilities, such as low education, substance use, or childhood trauma,
interact with relational dynamics like marital conflict and power imbalances, which are
in turn shaped by community factors including poverty, social norms, and weak social
support systems. Societal determinants, including legal frameworks, cultural
expectations, and gender hierarchies, further influence the prevalence and severity of
GBV. This ecological perspective emphasizes that effective interventions must operate
across multiple levels, integrating policy reform, community mobilization, and
individual support. While comprehensive, Krug et al. (2002) argue that ecological
models are sometimes applied superficially, lacking detailed examination of how
structural inequalities and cultural norms interact with individual and relational
behaviors, leaving gaps in explanatory depth.
Power and Control Theory
Power and control theory, particularly.as developed through the Duluth Model (Pence
& Paymar, 1993), complements these perspectives by focusing on intimate partner
dynamics. Violence, in this framework, is not a spontaneous expression of anger but a
deliberate strategy to assert and maintain control. Stark (2007) emphasizes that
coercive control--encompassing emotional, psychological, economic, and physical
85

[Page 77]
abuse--is a central feature of abusive relationships. This framework illuminates the
mechanisms through which perpetrators maintain dominance, suggesting that.
interventions must prioritize accountability, victim support, and empowerment
strategies.
Cultural and Normative Theories
Cultural and normative theories further elucidate the role of social values, traditions,
and norms in perpetuating GBV. Parsons (1951) and WHO (2002) highlight that certain
practices, such as early marriage, bride price, or acceptance of corporal punishment,
are socially sanctioned and thus reinforce male authority. Kandiyoti (1988) introduces
the concept of patriarchal bargaining, showing that women in many contexts negotiate
power within restrictive cultural frameworks, revealing the interplay between agency
and constraint. Cultural theory emphasizes that effective interventions must address
entrenched social attitudes, mobilize communities, and promote educational and
normative change. However, critics note that focusing exclusively on cultural norms
may neglect structural inequalities, individual psychological factors, and legal
frameworks that also shape GBV.
Conflictand MarxistPerspectives
Conflict and Marxist perspectives situate GBV within broader social and economic
private property and economic dependence, arguing that male dominance is reinforced
through economic power. Gelles (1983) observed that financial stress, poverty, and
economic dependence exacerbate family conflict and increase vulnerability to abuse.
Conflict theory underscores the importance of socioeconomic interventions, including
women's economic empowerment and poverty reduction, in mitigating GBV. Yet, as
Heise (1998) notes, economic explanations alone cannot account for the persistence of
violence in societies with varying economic conditions, highlighting the need to
integrate economic analysis with cultural, relational, and psychological insights.
Psychological Perspectives
Psychological perspectives complement these approaches by examining individual-
level determinants of GBV. Frustration-aggression theory (Dollard et al., 1939) and
clinical studies by. Dutton (1995) emphasize how personality traits, emotional
regulation, and trauma history contribute to violent behaviors. Childhood exposure to
abuse, substance use, and poor coping mechanisms are identified as significant risk
factors. While these insights inform interventions such as counselling and
rehabilitation, they must be considered alongside structural and cultural determinants
to avoid over-individualization of GBV causation.
Human Rights Perspective
The human rights perspective reframes GBV as a violation of fundamental human
rights, emphasizing state responsibility for protection and legal accountability (United
Nations, i993; Merry, 2006). This approach has been pivotal in promoting legal
86

[Page 78]
frameworks and international advocacy for GBV prevention. However, human rights
approaches often remain insufficiently integrated with socio-cultural and behavioral
theories, limiting their capacity to address underlying causes and community-level
dynamics (WHO,2002).

Forms of Gender-Based Violence
Gender-Based Violence can be grouped into tivo broad categories: physical and mental.
These categories cover most of the ways GBV manifests, although there are other
additional forms that extend beyond them.
Physical Forms
Physical forms involve direct bodily harm. This includes beating, slapping, and other
assaults.A husband hiting his wife during arguments, are common illustrations. Sexual
violence also belongs here, covering rape, sexual assault, and harassment. For example,
a female student coerced by a lecturer into sexual relations in exchange for grades, or
a boy abused by an older relative, both represent physical violations. Harmful
traditional practices are another physical form. Female genital mutilation (FGM) is a
striking example. Importantly, this practice is not carried out by men against women;
rather, it is often older women who perform it on younger girls, believing it preserves
purity or prepares them for marriage. The act causes severe physical pain, long-term
health complications, and psychological trauma
MentalForms
Mental forms involve emotional abuse, intimidation, humiliation, and controlling
behavior. A partner constantly belittling their spouse, restricting their freedom of 
movement, or threatening abandonment to instill fear are clear examples. Boys may
also suffer when parents mock them for expressing emotions, leaving long-term
psychological scars. Economic violence is another mental form, where individuals are
denied access to financial resources, employment, or property because of gender. For
instance, a widow, who even had children with her deceased husband, being stripped
of her husband's land by in-laws, or a man denied parental leave because caregiving is
seen as “women's work." Sexual harassment also fits here, as it often involves
unwanted comments, gestures, or innuendos that degrade dignity without necessarily
involving physical contact.
Cyber violence (sometimes called online GBV) and practices like dragging (public
shaming or coordinated online harassment) is another issue of Gender-Based Violence
under the mental forms category. Cyber violence primarily targets the mind, emotions,
and dignity rather than the body. It also involves intimidation, humiliation, threats, and
harassment carried out through digital platforms.

United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 '
The importance of women in peace and security is increasingly acknowledged globally.
Historically viewed primarily as victims of conflict, women are now recognized for
their essential roles in conflict prevention and peace processes, largely due to United
Nations Security Council Resolution 1325, adopted in October 2000. This resolution
emphasizes the distinct impact of armed conflict on women and girls, and the necessity
of their participation in decision-making for sustainable peace. It urges international
bodies and member states to integrate gender considerations into security strategies.
The work explores the Women, Peace, and Security framework, focusing on the pillars
and implementation of Resolution 1325 and the influences of earlier frameworks like
the Beijing Platform for Action (1995) and the Declaration on the Elimination of
Violence against Women (1993).
1. Women, Peace and Security (WPS) Agenda
Decades of advocacy by international and women's organizations led to the
establishment of the Women, Peace, and Security (WPS) agenda, framed by the United
Nations Security Council Resolution 1325, which recognizes women's essential roles
in conflict prevention and peacebuilding.
2. The Five Pillars of UN Security Council Resolution 1325
Although the original framework identified four pillars, many policy frameworks later
expanded it to five key pillars to strengthen implementation.
2.1 Participation
The inclusion of women in decision-making processes, particularly in peace talks and
conflict resolution, enhances the effectiveness of peace agreements. The resolution
calls for member nations to increase women's participation in peace and security
organizations, recognizing that women provide valuable perspectives on social welfare,
community security, and reconciliation.
2.2Prevention
Preventing violence against women and girls is a primary goal ofthe preventative pillar,
prevention plans and peacekeeping missions. Strategies include gender-sensiive
conflict analysis, awareness campaigns, and promoting women's leadership in
mediation.

2.5Recovery
Recovery highlights women's contributions to social, economic, and post-conflict
reconstruction. It promotes women's involvement in the post-conflict reconstruction of
institutions, economic systems, and governance frameworks. This pillar also supports
initiatives to empower women economically and socially in post-conflict cultures.
3.Implementation of Resolution1325
The implementation of the United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 occurs
 through multiple mechanisms at the international, regional, and national levels.
3.1 National Action Plans (NAPs)
To achieve the WPS objective, some nations have developed National Action Plans.
These programs include tactics to safeguard women from violence, increase women's
participation in peace processes, and incorporate gender perspectives into national
security initiatives.
3.2Organizations of the United Nations
The Department of Peacekeeping Operations and UN Women are crucial to the
implementation of the resolution. They offer training courses for soldiers and mediators
and encourage gender mainstreaming in peacekeeping operations.
4. The 1993 Declaration on the Elimination of Violence Against Women
One of the first international documents expressly addressing violence against women
was the United Nations General Assembly's 1993 adoption of the Declaration on the
Elimination of Violence Against Women. According to the Declaration, violence
against women is any act of gender-based violence that causes women to suffer
physically, sexually, or psychologically, whether it takes place in a private or public
setting. Since it acknowledges that historically unequal power dynamics between men
and women are the root cause of violence against women, it urges governments to:
 Develop laws and policies to prevent violence against women
Protect victims and provide support services

prevention and peacebuilding. It establishes a framework focusing on five pillars:

prevent and punish all forms of GBV, ensuring accessibility and sensitivity to
the needs of survivors.
2. Prioritize Survivor Leadership: Design interventions that empower survivors
to actively participate in decision-making, advocacy, and community
reintegrationprocesses.
3. Engage Communities and Faith Leaders: Collaborate with local
communities, traditional authorities, and religious organizations to challenge
harmful gender norms and promote non-violence.
4. Institutionalize Women's Participation in Peacebuilding: Guarantee
women's representation in peace negotiations, governance, and post-conflict
reconstruction through formal policies and dedicated programs.
5. Address,Socio-Economic Inequalities: Implement initiatives. to improve
women's access to education, economic opportunities, and healthcare to reduce
vulnerability to GBV and enhance social equity.
6. Decolonize Peace and Justice Systems: Integrate local knowledge,
experiences, and leadership from the Global South into international peace and
justice frameworks to ensure culturally relevant and effective interventions.
7.
Secure Sustainable Funding: Allocate long-terim, flexible funding for GBV
prevention, response, and survivor support, recognizing the importance of
continuity in achieving lasting impact.
8. Promote Education and Awareness: Conduct awareness campaigns and
educational programs to foster gender equality, non-violent conflict resolution,
and respect for human rights across all age groups.
References
Aldajani, S., & Leiner, S. (2022). Conflict transformation approaches. Peacebuilding
Journal, 10(3), 201-218.
Amadiume, I. (1987). Male daughters, female husbands: Gender and sex in an African
society. London: Zed Books.

chapters.content:
[Page 88]
CHAPTERSIX
HealthandConflict
Y. Adevoyinl K. Leweanyal O. P. Anierobil J. C. Onul V C. Nivaeze
Introduction
from where the individuals intend to access care, to conflicts among the health
professionals from whom the individuals would receive care; the nature and type of
care to be offered; and the individuals' disposition to the offers based on past
experiences, religious beliefs, cultural disposition and personal beliefs. On the other
hand, conflicts, too, have health consequences.
During physical and emotional confrontation between individuals, victims require care
to restore their health. In times of social unrests, civil disturbances and war, casualties
require treatment. In instances where forced displacement during conflicts turns the
population into refugees, healthcare issues among the refugees are a consequence of
conflict. The relationship between health and conflict is, therefore, bidirectional. In this
chapter, we discuss the relationships in three sections. The first section deals with issues
around conflicts in health facilities provision and utilization, the second looks at
conflicts in healthcare delivery, while the third section focuses on health in conflict
situations. Before the discussing the relationships, however, we provide a conceptual
lens for understanding the key concept, health, as well as its associated concepts of
diseaseandillness.
Health, Disease and Illness - A Conceptual Clarification
In 1946, the World Health Organization (WHO) defined health, as a state of complete
physical, mental, and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or
infirmity (WHO, 1946). This definition was heavily criticized on the grounds that it
was utopian, inflexible, and unrealistic (Meade et al, 1988; Godlee, 201l; Awofeso,
2012). Following from such criticisms, a number of definitions for the term health'
have since emerged. Dolfman (1973) explained that the word health'was derived from
the old English word 'hoelth', which meant a state of being sound, and was generlly
used to infer a soundness of the body. Parsons (1972) then defined health as the state
of optimum capacity of an individual for the effective performance of the roles and
demands of life commensurate with age, culture, and personal responsibility.

[Page 89]
disease or disability while the wellness model defines health with regards to health
discomfort, or disability. Of the several definitions of disease, Boorse's (1977)
They go further to describe seven major themes in discussing what disease entails.
These are pain, suffering and discomfort; treatment by physicians; statistical normality;
disability; adaptation; homeostasis; and value. According to Boorse (1977), disease
unbearable and thus requires palliative care. Some pains, sufferings and discomforts
which cannot be termed as disease however include teething, menstruation and
childbirth. Disease should also be treatable medically. Treatment could be in the form
of drugs administration and therapeutic procedures to cure or manage ailments.
Statistical normality in explaining disease, according to Boorse (1977), requires the use
of specie's average measurement levels on certain indicators as a yardstick for
measuring normality and deviation from normality. Such measures include blood
pressure, basal metabolism, weight, sugar level, height, pulse, and respiration. Any
measure outside the normal range is usually termed as a disease condition. Disease
could also lead to many forms of disability. Poliomyelitis, for instance, can cause
physical deformities of the limbs. Being able to adapt to the environment is a form of
healthiness while those who are not fit or able to adapt are presumably diseased.
Disease is also a state of homeostatic imbalance or failure. With respect to value as a
theme in explaining disease, disease is seen as undesirable while health is desirable.
Being free from disease is thus a social value in human society.
Aclosely related concept to the concept ofdisease isillness. Ilness is a situation when
an individual consciously feels that they are unhealthy as a result of pain and discomfort
(Parsons, 1951). Amzat and Razum (2014) describe illness as a manifestation of a
diseased condition. That is, a diseased person might not be aware or conscious that they
have a disease until such an individual presents with a situationwhere-they are unable
to function normally.Illness is thus about a disability to function normally and to be
self-aware ofthat disability to function. It is a progression from the mere presence of a
medical problem or condition (disease) to the presentation of disabling symptoms and
signs. This implies that it is possible to have a disease without being illand that disease
101

[Page 90]
makes people ill (Amzat & Razum, 2014). While disease is a form of medical problem
in the human body and system, illness is a manifestation of such medical problem.
Conflicts inHealth
Health is a public good. Public goods are those goods and services to which the public
have access and which they are able to consume without reducing the quantity available
for others to consume. They are usually provided by the government to address welfare
concerns and/or to address market failures occasioned by private sector provisions
(Lipsey & Chrystal, 2004). Public goods have two main characteristics. They are non-
excludable -and non-rivalrous (Cowen, 1997; Lipsey & Chrystal, 2004). Non-
excludability implies that no single individual can be excluded from consuming the
goods or services-after-they have been provided. Roads built by the government for the
public are a typical example. Party affiliations, religion, gender or any other
discriminatory factor cannot be used to stop any member of the public from using the
roads. A good is non-rivalrous when the consumption by an individual does not reduce
the units available-for others to consume; street lightning, education and police services
for instance: Government hospitals and the health personnel in them are examples of
public goods.
Siting a healthcare facility generates conflicts when there are contestations over where
such facility should be located. This stems from the fact that the location of such
facilities confers some forms of advantages on people living in close proximity to the
facilities (Adewoyin et al, 2018). Studies have also shown that distance travelled is a
major determinant of health facilities utilization as many individuals would rather
patronize the facilities closest to them for basic health seeking (Adewoyin 2017;
Abdulmageed & Elnimeiri, 2018; Kifle et al, 2018; Johnson et al, 2020). As such,
communities, groups and influential individuals within the communities, lobby
government to attract the facility to their locations, and, in the process, may ignite
conflicts with other communities, groups and individuals seeking to attract the same
facility to their own location. Population distribution and need are the main distributive
factors of public goods in Nigeria. Other factors include political consideration and
socialclass.
Beyond providing public healthcare facilities and determining where they are located,
the operational licences and location of private health facilities through the ministries
of health and urban and regional planning respectively. More importantly, governments
are also responsible for ethical goverrance issues, including those with potential
implications for conflicts. Ethical issues in human healthcare provision include the
legal, moral and social implications of advances in biomedical research and technology
in the treatment of illnesses and diseases and in the general provision of healthcare.
Some healthcare issues falling within the scope of ethical governance are abortion,
organ donation, organ transplant, assisted reproduction and invitro fertilization (IVF),
the use of human subjects for experiments and research, gene therapy and genetic
102

[Page 91]
unintended consequences of some of these advancements.
For example, when Dolly, a sheep, was cloned in 1996, the reactions in the scientific
possible to clone humans; how long would the world have to wait to see a human clone;
Similarly, while IVFs have helped many families deal with childlessness, there exists
a societal stigma associated with ‘test tube' babies in certain societies (Upton, 2023),
especially with couples who used either or both of donor eggs and sperm. Mediating
the conflicting and opposing viewpoints made the issue of ethical governance
Pahang, 2023). In other words, in providing healthcare, the patient's rights to make
their own decision and choices must be respected, the care must be done in a way as to
benefit others and avoid harm to them, and there must be a fair and equitable
distribution of resources and opportunities.
Notivithstanding the principles, governments have the right to take healthcare decisions
on behalf of their population and in the public interest. When individuals exercise their
rights to patient's autonomy and their decision goes in conflict with the public interest
as envisioned by the government, governments may impose restrictions or resort to
moral suasion. For example, the government of Nigeria took a decision to vaccinate
children in a global polio eradication drive. The initiative suffered a setback in Nigeria
in 2003 when members of the Hausa-Fulani ethnic group staged a boycott on the
suspicion that the vaccines allegedly contained anti-fertility agents to reduce the future
population of the North (Yahya, 2007; Olufowote, 2011). The suspicion wasn't out of
place as the polio immunization exercise was concentrated largely in the North. But
then, the North was the region where the virus was most endemic.
In the recent past, many individuals also objected to getting Covid-19 vaccination, even
though the government saw vaccination against Covid-19 as being in the public
interest. The government could only bar unvaccinated people from entering certain
public facilities or enjoying some privileges while appealing to their sense of morality.
Members of the Jehovah's Witnesses religious group are also renowned for their
aversion to blood transfusion, even in the face of critical injuries requiring same. The
medical personnel providing them with care must respect their ability to decide on their
choice of treatment to avoid conflicts. To avoid infringing on individual choices and
prevent conflicts, healthcare providers require informed consent from the patients or,
in the event of their incapacitation, their next of kin.
Because some ofthe ethical conflicts in health transcend individuals and could happen
at the level of national governments, ethical governance framework also exists at a
103

[Page 92]
supranational level. For example, countries of the world were divided in their support
for cloning (Langlois, 2017). While countries who 'support it may derive certain
beneftsfromi,thenegativeconsequences may be tranboundary innature, withmore
intergovernmental level are domiciled with the United Nations Educational, Scientific
and Cultural Organization (UNICEF). Examples ofthe United Nations' framework for
preventing conflicts in health through ethics are the Universal Declaration on Bioethics
and Human Rights, the Declaration on Human Cloning, and the Universal Declaration
on'the Human Genome and Human Rights. The last being with respect to ethical ssues
yardsticks are used to determine which genes are normal or abnormal; what human
traits should not be modified; what are its application limits - like using it to enhance
intelligence, agility, height etc. rather than for disease treatment and so on.
HealthcareDeliveryConflicts
Healthcare delivery conflicts refer to disagreements, tensions or disputes that occur
within the healthcare systems involving healthcare professionals, patients, institutions
effectiveness, organizational efficiency and overall healthcare outcomes (Baker &
Moore, 2013). Understanding these conflicts and developing strategies for resolution
is critical for ensuring high-quality healthcare delivery and mental health situation.
Reeves et al (2017) observed that healthcare delivery conflicts manifest in different
forms. Inter-professional, patient-provider, institutional and systemic conflicts are
some notable examples of conflicts in the delivery of healthcare.
Inter-professional conflict' is the type of conflict between different healthcare
professionals (doctors, nurses, pharmacists, social workers etc.) which can arise due to
differences in roles, responsibilities, professional training, and communication styles.
. A physician might override the decisions of a nurse or there may be disagreements
about treatment approaches between specialists and generalists. In other words,
disagreements or tensions may arise within the same healthcare profession. It could
also be a dispute between two nurses over patient care priorities or a conflict between
a 'senior surgeon and a junior colleague about treatment methods. Patient-provider
conflict, on its part, occurs between patients and healthcare providers, often due to
misunderstandings, communication issues or differences in expectations. Patients may.
feel that their concerns are not being heard or they may disagree with the prescribed
treatment or the quality of care they are receiving (Hughes, 2014).
An aspect of the patient-provider conflict worth expanding on is the peculiarity of
patients battling drug abuse and mental health disorders. Individuals struggling with
substance use and mental health issues often experience heightened emotional distress,
impaired decision-making and challenges in managing relationships. They also
experience an inability to communicate effectively (Weisner and Greenfield, 2016).
104

[Page 93]
These can lead to conflicts with family members, peers, colleagues and healthcare
providers. When individuals are unable to regulate their emotions, they may react
impulsively or aggressively. leading to interpersonal conflict. During provider-patient
conflict, healthcare providers may become frustrated when patients do not adhere to
treatment plans, particularly if substance abuse interferes with mental health treatment.
This can create a cycle of conflict between patients and providers, where patients may
feel judged or misunderstood, while providers may feel helpless or exhausted from
managing challenging cases.
Institutional conflicts arise within or between healthcare institutions, often related to
policies, resource allocation, organizational priorities or staffing issues. Examples
include conflicts between hospital administration and medical staff over budget cuts,
that occur at the level of healthcare systems, involving disagreements between
governmental bodies, insurers, healthcare providers and the public. Issues such as
healthcare access, insurance coverage and the distribution of resources can lead to
systemic conflicts that affect the delivery of care. Overall, the commonest causes of
healthcare delivery conflicts include role ambiguity, power dynamics, differences in
professional training, poor communication and conflict of interests.
Different healthcare professionals may have unclear or overlapping roles, leading to
confusion about who is responsible for what.A nurse might feel that a physician is
encroaching on their duties or a physician may feel that they are not getting the support
they need from other healthcare team members. Power dynamics emanating from
hierarchical structures in healthcare organizations can create power imbalances,
leading to frustration and resistance among lower-ranked staff members. Senior
physicians may hold more authority than nurses or allied health professionals, which
can lead to tension and hinder collaboration (Lohfeld et al, 2017). There are also
differences in professional training and perspectives among healthcare professionals
from different disciplines. These are consequent on the different training philosophies,
approaches to patient care and problem-solving methods.Asurgeon might focus on the
technical aspects of a patient's condition while a social worker may emphasize the
patient's social and emotional needs. These differences can lead to conflicts over
treatmentpriorities.
Issues like poor communication, whether verbal or non-verbal, can escalate
misunderstandings and create confict, In healthcare settings, where teams oen work
in high-pressure environments,ineffective communication between team members can
lead to erors, confusion and frustration (Hughes, 2014). Resource constraints due to
limited resources such as time, funding, equipment and staff is yet another pressure.
When resources are scarce, competition for these resources can create tension between
team members, departments or institutions. Conflict of interests among different
healthcare providers or stakeholders often leads to conflict.A physician may prioritize
medical outcomes, while a nurse may prioritize patient comfort. Additionally,
105

[Page 94]
insurance companies may have different priorities than healthcare providers, creating
a conflict over treatment plans. Cultural and personality differences between team
members or between providers and patients can lead to misunderstandings or perceived
disrespect (Stone & Stone, 2016). For example, a healthcare provider from one cultural
background may have a communication style that clashes with a patient from another
background, leading to conflict.
Healthcare delivery conflicts impact negatively on the healthcare system in deferent
ways. Conflicts can lead to fragmented care, delayed interventions and inconsistent
treatment plans, all of which can negatively affect patient outcomes. Communication
problem between a nurse and a physician could result in a medication error, affecting
the patient's health. Decrease in team collaboration can erode trust and cooperation
within healthcare teams. As team members become more focused on their individual
perspectives, teamwork and collaboration can suffer, leading to inefficiencies and
errors (Reeves et al, 2017). Healthcare professionals working in a conflict-ridden
environment are more likely to experience stress, frustration and burnout (Baker &
Moore, 2013).
High levels of workplace conflict can contribute to job dissatisfaction, absenteeism and
high staff turnover rate, further destabilizing healthcare teams and ultimately affecting
patient's experience of care. Effective teamwork is essential for high-quality care and
conflict can undermine it. Poor communication, lack of collaboration and fractured
team dynamics can lead to suboptimal decision-making and patient care. Persistent
conflict can foster a toxic work environment where staff members feel undervalued,
unsupported or disillusioned. This can lead to a cycle of low morale, poor performance
and high turnover, all of which negatively affect the institution's ability to provide
qualitycare.
. Healthcare delivery conflicts are natural but a potentially disruptive part of the complex
 and high-stakes environment in which healthcare professionals operate. Understanding
the causes and impacts of these conflicts is essential to creating an environment that
promotes collaboration, respect and quality patient care. By proactively addressing
conflict through clear communication, role clarity, conflict resolution training and
strong leadership, healthcare teams can reduce the negative impacts of conflict and
work more effectively toward common goals. In turn, this fosters better patient
outcomes, improved team dynamics and a more supportive healthcare environment. By
also promoting cultural sensitivity, religious respect and human rights in care,
healthcare providers can create environments where individuals feel safe, supported
and respected in their recovery journey. Conflict resolution,"when handled
HealthinConflicts
Conflict situations profoundly affect the health and well-being of affected populations,
often causing widespread suffering and overwhelming health systems. From injuries
106

[Page 95]
and disease outbreaks to mental health crises, the consequences oflarge-scale conflicts,
like war, extend far beyond the batlefield, impacting the lives of civilians, healthcare
workers, and vulnerable communities. The health challenges in conflict zones can be
categorized into direct and indirect consequences. Direct impacts include physical
injuries such as gunshot wounds, shrapnel injuries, and burns caused by violence or
bombings. War also destroys healthcare infrastructure, reducing access to essential
services and supplies. Indirectly, conflicts lead to disease outbreaks, as displacement,
overcrowding, and poor sanitation create fertile conditions for the spread of infectious
diseases such as cholera, malaria, and respiratory infections (Akresh etal, 2012).
According to Singh et al (2019), for displaced people, who are often times housed in
refugee camps, overcrowding, poor sanitation, and limited access to clean water in the
internally displaced persons (IDP) and refugee camps create ideal conditions for the
spread of infectious diseases. Waterborne illnesses such as cholera and dysentery are
common due to unsafe drinking water and inadequate waste disposal systems.
Respiratory infections like pneumonia and tuberculosis spread rapidly in crowded
environments, while vector-borne diseases such as malaria and dengue are prevalent in
tropical regions. Low immunization rates also make camp residents susceptible to
outbreaks of vacine-preventable diseases, including measles and polio. Overwhelmed
healthcare systems in these settings often struggle to contain such outbreaks.fi
Maternal and child health is severely compromised due to the disruption of prenatal
care and safe delivery services, often leading to increased mortality rates. Additionally,
chronic diseases like diabetes and hypertension are neglected during conflicts, resulting
in severe complications for affected individuals (Dunn, 2018). Mental health also
emerges as a significant concern. Survivors of conflict often experience post-traumatic
stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, and depression. The psychological toll is exacerbated
by the loss of loved ones, homes, and livelihoods, further undermining the overall well-
being of affected populations (Akresh et al, 2012). Food insecurity, caused by disrupted
supply chains and agricultural activities, leads to malnutrition, particularly among
children and pregnant women (Igreja et al, 2021). Women and girls are at an increased
risk of sexual violence, exploitation, and abuse. Survivors of violence often face
physical injuries, sexualy transmtted infections, and long-term psychological trauma
Conflict-induced migration forces millions of people to flee their homes in search of
safety, ofen under dire conditions. Migrants escaping conflict face unique health
challenges that arise from the circumstances of their displacement, the journey to
consequences of conflicts highlighted above, conflict-induced migrants face additional
burden of physical trauma and injuries sustained during their escape. Wounds from
violence, accidents, orexposure to dangerous terrains oen gountreated due toa lack
of immediate medical care during their journey. They are also faced with challenges in
oftenlacking the capacity tomeet the needsoflargenumbersofmigrants; lackoflegal
107

[Page 96]
status or financial resources to access healthcare services; cultural and language
differences, which may lead to miscommunication and cultural misunderstandings; and
Healthcare Interventions and Barriers in Conflict Situations.
Addressing health in confict zones requires a multifaceted approach, combining
(Ibaniez & Velez, 2021) and long-term resilience-building efforts. Emergency medical
care is a critical first step, focusing on treating trauma, managing infections, and
stabilizing patients. Field hospitals and mobile clinics play a vital role in delivering
care in areas where traditional healthcare infrastructure has collapsed, Preventing
disease outbreaks is another essential intervention. Vaccination campaigns against
diseases like measles and cholera are crucial, especially in overcrowded settings like
refugee and IDP camps. Clean water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) programs help
prevent the spread of waterborne diseases, while vector control measures, such as
distributing insecticide-treated bed nets, reduce the risk of malaria (Grundy et al, 2018).
Maternal and child health services are also a priority. Mobile maternity units and
emergency obstetric care ensure safe deliveries, while nutritional programs address
malnutrition in children and pregnant women. Mental health support is increasingly
integrated into healthcare responses, with trauma counselling and community-based
programs helping to address the psychological toll of conflict (Elbadawi & Sambanis,
2021). International organizations play a vital role in health responses during conflicts.
The World Health Organization (WHO) coordinates public health efforts, provides
medical supplies, and advises on rebuilding health systems. Medecins Sans Frontieres
(MSF) specializes in emergency medical care, while the International Committee of
the Red Cross (ICRC) delivers healthcare in war zones and advocates for the protection
of medical personnel under international humanitarian law. UN agencies like UNICEF
and UNFPA focus on specific aspects of health, such as child immunizations, nutrition,
governments, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and community leaders to
ensure effective and sustainable healthcare delivery (Garfield et al 2020).
Healthcare delivery during war is, however, fraught with challenges. One of the most
significant barriers is the destruction of hospitals and clinics, which leaves many
communities without access to essential services. The destruction of hospitals and
clinics, coupled with the displacement or targeting of healthcare workers, leads to a
severe shortage of medical services. Medical supplies are often scarce, and healthcare
workers may flee, be displaced, or become targets themselves (Ityavyar & Ogba, 2019).
Services for survivors of sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) are frequently
inadequate or inaccessible (Grundy, 2022).
Medical supplies, vaccines, and basic equipment are often unavailable, leaving
108

[Page 97]
blockades, damaged infrastructure, and ongoing security threats. Patients in need of
urgent care are often unable to reach medical facilities, while humanitarian
areas, In addition tothese logistical challenges, cultural and systemic barriers also
affect healthcare delivery. Stigma surrounding mental health or sexual violence may
prevent individuals from seeking help.Furthermore,underfunding ofhealth initiatives
in conflict zones limits the scope and quality of availableservices (Ityavyar& Ogba
2019). The lack of funding and limited humanitarian access also hinder efforts to
provide adequate care (Goodhand, 2023).
Approaches to Health and Treatnent in War Zones 
Healthcare interventions in war zones focus on addressing immediate needs while
laying the groundwork for long-term recovery. Building on Jolem (2021), some
approaches to health treatment in war zone are as follow:
Emergency and Trauma Care
Emergency medical care is the first priority in war situations. Field hospitals, mobile
clinics, and triage systems are critical for stabilizing patients and providing life-saving
interventions. This includes surgery for severe injuries, treatment of burns, and
rehabilitation services for amputees and others with long-term physical impairments.
Disease Prevention and Management
Preventing disease outbreaks is crucial in. conflict settings. Vaccination campaigns
against diseases like cholera and measles are essential, particularly in refugee and IDP
camps. Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) programs help prevent the spread of
waterborne diseases, while vector control measures, such as insecticide-treated bed
nets, reduce the risk of malaria.
Maternaland Child Health
therapeutic foods and essential vitamins to combat imalnutrition. Infant and young child
feeding (IYCF) programs promote breastfeeding and complementary feeding practices
to improve child health outcomes.
Sexual and Reproductive Health
Reproductive health services, including access to contraceptives, emergency obstetric
reproductive health rights and services empower women and girls to'seek care.
Mental Health and Psychosocial Support
Mental health services are increasingly recognized as vital in war zones. Psychological
first aid and trauma counselling are provided alongside medical care to address the
109

[Page 98]
psychological toll of war. Community-based mental health programs and training
healthcare workers in basic mental health interventions help support affected
populations.
Nutritional Support
Nutritional programs address both acute and chronic malnutrition. Severely
malnourished children are treated with ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTF), while
supplementary feeding programs provide essential nutrients to pregnant and lactating
women. Food security is bolstered through the provision of culturally appropriate food
aid.
ManagementofChronicDiseases
Continuity of care for chronic conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, and epilepsy
is often overlooked in emergencies. Training local healthcare providers and supplying
essential medications can prevent complications and improve long-term outcomes.
The approaches can be delivered through a combination of mechanisms. These,
according to Tran (2020), based on their work on the Angolan civil war that lasted for
over 26 years, include mobile clinics to bring healthcare services to remote or
overcrowded sections of camps, providing essential care to those who might otherwise
lack access. Training camp residents as community health workers also helps extend
the reach of healthcare services. These workers educate their peers, monitor health
conditions, and provide basic care. Collaboration between international organizations,
local governments, and NGOs is another mechanism that ensures effective healthcare
delivery. Organizations like UNHCR, WHO, and Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) play
key roles in providing health services, disease surveillance, and emergency response.
Conclusion
Conflicts are inevitable. How they are handled, and the consequences therefrom, make
the difference in outcomes. In the health space, conflicts arise in healthcare
provisioning, healthcare delivery, the choices individuals make in the utilization of
healthcare services, and among healthcare professionals in the course of providing
services. This chapter has also shown that healthcare conflicts abound between
governments of different countries, especially with regards to the handling and
management of advances in healthcare technology and its applications. Conflicts,
themselves, also have health consequences. Whether at individual levels or at the levels
of groups, communities or countries, victims of conflicts require healthcare to deal with
the trauma, injuries, diseases and illnesses emanating from the conflict situations. As
such, understanding the bidirectional relationship between health and conflict, as
detailed in this chapter, presents a veritable launchpad for mitigating and resolving
health conflicts.,
110

chapters.title: Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
chapters.content:
[Page 99]
ChapterSeven
Conflict Analysis and Framework Assessment
Introduction
of success or failure in interventions is based on the intervener(s) knowledge of the
dispute.
It is important to recognise that conflict is not inherently bad or destructive; yet, it is
essential to assert that unmanaged conflict can become a volatile situation with the
managed to prevent escalation into violence. It is important to note that choosing an
appropriate method for. managing conflict is preceded by a proper analysis of the
particular conflict scenario. In other words, central to the factors that can enhance
successful conflict management, resolution, and transformation, or that can lead to their
failure, is conflict analysis. Conflict analysis is the methodical examination of the
characteristics, origins, participants, and dynamics of conflict (IDASA, 2004).
Consequently, a comprehensive understanding of the nature and dynamics of conflict
is essential to evaluate its potential and determine the appropriate course of action. As
such, this chapters aims to provide the reader and prospective conflict interveners with
the tools necessary for the successful analysis of any conflict situation. We aim to
accomplish this objective by elucidating the 'what', 'why', and 'how' of conflict analysis.
This endeavour does not in any way imply that this chapter is exhaustive. Rather, it
aims to encapsulate pertinent aspects of conflict analysis in a condensed format. We
begin by elucidating the concept of conflict analysis.
What constitutes Conflict Analysis?ijea
A superficial examination of the term "conflict analysis" indicates it is a composite of
the two.syllables"conflict" and "analysis". Due to space constraints, readers are urged
to focus on the discussions of conflict presented in the preceding chapters of this
collection. Let us proceed to the subsequent topic - analysis. The term 'analysis' is
defined by the Oxford Advanced Learners Dictionary as a 'meticulous study or
examination of a subject to gain deeper understanding' Therefore, 'to analyse' entails
scrutinising the nature or structure of an entity to enhance comprehension or
elucidation. It involves an elucidation and clarification of a certain phenomenon.
114

[Page 100]
investigationofaproblen intendedtyieldastructured andmethodicalcomprehension
of particular topics under consideration.
Fisher et al. (2000) conceived of conflict analysis as involving the systematic
examination and comprehension ofthe conflict's reality from multipleviewpoints.This
unequivocally positions conflict analysis as an action-oriented endeavour aimed at
comprehending the nature, causes, and dynamics of a specific conflict for diverse
objectives. Madu (2015) perceives conflict analysis as a method for acquiring a
comprehensive understanding of the dynamics, nature, characteristics, issues, and
context ofthe conflict, along with the involved parties and their relationships within
the dispute. Consequently, it constitutes the methodical examination of the
characteristies, origins, participants, and dynamics of conflicts (IDASA, 2004).
By its nature,'conflict is a dynamic phenomenon. As such, no two confrontations are
identical. The distinctiveness of each conflict and its circumstances underscores the
importance of conflict analysis. Conflict analysis provides conflict managers with a
comprehensive grasp of the dispute. The fundamental premise of conflict analysis is
that, despite the distinct characteristics of each dispute, there exist shared theoretical
concepts for comprehending and addressing them. This assumption presupposes that
conflict analysis largely focuses on the reaction patterns of third parties to conflict
situations. Conflict analysis precedes conflict intervention. It is a pragmatic instrument
that assists conflict managers in efficiently devising their intervention strategies.
Consequently, conflict analysis is essential as it is the initial phase of conflict
intervention, resolution, and change. Effective conflict prevention and resolution
necessitate an analysis of the causes, triggers, dynamics, and patterns of conflict, along
with the elements and societal dynamics that enhance resilience to conflict. Early
analysis and continuous monitoring are crucial for predicting conflict and altering
conflict dynamics to empower people and social organisations dedicated to non-violent
conflict resolution (Sandole, et al., 2009).
Furthermore, conflict analysis constitutes one of the three fundamental components of
peace practice. The remaining two are conflict tracking and conflict intervention
(IDASA, 2004). The phrase "Peace Practice" encompasses the full range of
peacekeeping, peace-making, and peacebuilding, together refrred to as the Peace
Process. It encompasses conflict resolution, conflict management, and any related
teriminology pertinent to the discourse on preventing, managing, alleviating, and
controlling societal conflicts (IDASA, 2004). It is the systematic method of conflict
resolution and peaceful advancement. It entails controlling detrimental conflicts and
fostering constructive conflicts to achieve positive peace. The process necessitates
comprehension of the mechanisms of emerging or existing conflict (conflict
sensitisation) and peace education; non-violent confrontation and community
mobilisation; ongoing debate and negotiation; as well as healing and peaceful
development (IDASA, 2004).
